The bigger the dimension is, the harder to fit, the model to the data. But here, the action space is quite large, but we did very good job to make sure the model fits well and gives you a smooth-

Swyx [00:45:10]: Can you bound the order of magnitude of the action space, or is that-

Jason Ma [00:45:14]: Yeah, so it’s on the order of, about a hundred action dimensions.

Swyx [00:45:19]: Yeah, and these are all continuou- continuous, right?

Jason Ma [00:45:21]: Continuous, right. So the model is just basically predicting at very high frequency, like tens, like at least fifty-dimensional vector, like ten, twenty times a second to get that continuous motion.

Swyx [00:45:34]: And potentially predicting one to two seconds out, so that is another hundred frames or whatever.

Jason Ma [00:45:39]: Of course.

Vibhu [00:45:40]: There’s a bit of a history, similar to context of previous state, I guess.

Jason Ma [00:45:45]: So context is a very important thing in robotics, right? Because otherwise, if you’re just making decision based on the current observation, sometimes it’s really hard to tell what to do next, right? For example if you think about opening a microwave, like in the middle part, it’s unclear whether or not you’re-

Vibhu [00:46:01]: Closing

Jason Ma [00:46:01]: … closing or trying to open it, right? So context is also really important.

Swyx [00:46:05]: And I have a screenshot of the fridge demo where it is, there’s agentic planning and tool holding and all those things. So we can show that for listeners.

Vibhu [00:46:13]: I think that’s an interesting side. After the model-

Agentic Harnesses and Planning Physical Workflows

Vibhu [00:46:16]: … how do you wrap it around into agentic harness? Like, what is-

Swyx [00:46:22]: Claude Code

Vibhu [00:46:22]: … Claude Code deployment? Claude Code UI. You have a lot of cool UIs, but what goes into wrapping model output towards final thing? Is this custom per use case? Is it you have your own SDK?

Jason Ma [00:46:37]: So, eventually we will have our own SDK, but the way we think about is we want a general harness layer for robotics foundation model. Today, that is our own model, right? The way I think about is for any Real task, long task in the physical world, there is a lot of a high-level decision-making you have to do, right? It’s not just like robot, only reasoning about the physical world in the action, continuous trajectories, right? Because that’s a very low level, the thing you’re actually executing in the physical world, but that’s not the intent. But like if. When we are doing decision-making, we think about steps of a recipe. We think about, oh I finished this I need to do that. While I’m waiting for this part to finish, I need to go somewhere else to do something else. There’s a lot of high-level cognition, decision-making that’s happening. And I think for robots to handle even, the laundry task we are showing you, it has to have that capability. Because, it needs to reason that okay, the washer is running, so I should go do something else while the washer’s finishing. But now the washer is done, I should take, I should take the towels from the washer and put it in dryer immediately, right? Because if not, then that becomes a bottleneck in the whole workflow, right? So there is a lot of reasoning that needs to happen for robotics. And I think in theory, you could just, try to learn that with a low-level model that’s outputting actions, but it’ll be extremely inefficient. So that is why having a hierarchical system, like putting a harness, like an agentic system around our world action model is what allow the model to compose different capabilities, different skills to solve a much longer horizon task. It’s very much like in language model, right? Like two years ago, three years ago, the model was only good at autocomplete. Like, humans have to tap to get the model to keep spitting out code. But today, just an agentic system just carries the end-to-end task. And that’s. I, and I think that’s important because I think today in robotics, people are still thinking about autonomy at the very task level like one minute, thirty-second task. But really, the value is about tasks or workflows that go on unsupervised for hours. And that’s what we’re building towards. And that’s why I think thinking about. The robotics problem, not just as a modeling problem, but rather as a system problem, you need good agent, good harness engineer, good model, good hardware, everything. It’s like how we think general-purpose robots ought to be solved.

How Coding Agents Accelerate Robotics Research

Vibhu [00:49:07]: Do you guys see benefits from language model coding tools getting better? So new Opus 5.5, new Astra. Do you have language models in your agent harness? How does AGI being developed in language model space affect you guys?

Jason Ma [00:49:24]: No. Yeah, no, absolutely. Like, it affects us very deeply in many ways. One is that we are extremely AI-native company, right? Like, coding agents, all of that is a very fundamental part of our work, and we’re very welcoming of that. Like, whenever there’s a new model, we’re the first one to test it, right? Like, we being. Like, when GPT-6 came out, we had a company-wide hackathon the same week, and the thing that our engineers built was incredible. And many of them are— Many of the features we built is already in main, in production, right? So we really like using coding agents to accelerate our work.

Swyx [00:50:00]: Just for the people interested, anything surprising in GPT-6 that you found?

Jason Ma [00:50:05]: … it’s about the ability for it to construct virtual environments, right? Turns dissemination. We talked that twenty minutes ago. I think that’s really exciting.

Vibhu [00:50:17]: It’s interesting. There were so many CAD, Zillow to 3D-ish.

Swyx [00:50:21]: He lost the hackathon to the CAD, -

Vibhu [00:50:24]: I won the. I did the CAD bullshit. Other way.

Swyx [00:50:27]: No. Oh.

Vibhu [00:50:28]: That was. I won a GPT hackathon just for fun. I was like, “I know nothing CAD.” Might as well play around with it ‘cause every demo is doing it. I’m like, “It’s gonna be garbage.” And I’m like, “Well, it’s kinda grounded, it’s kinda good.” But it’s just hackathon stuff.

Deployment Milestones and Competing Robotics Strategies

Vibhu [00:50:45]:.

Swyx [00:50:45]: Cool. I wa— I was gonna round out, some of the use cases and then go into a little bit of company culture and your personal background.

Vibhu [00:50:52]: I have two technical questions. One is, are there any goals you wanna set for yourself, like six months, one year, two year timeline that you see robots should be able to do, fill in the blank, that you’re kinda working towards?

Jason Ma [00:51:09]: Yeah, in the six months to one year frame, our goal is definitely scaling up our robots and our model and truly getting them to deploy-

Vibhu [00:51:18]: Like a task.

Jason Ma [00:51:18]: … completely different.

Vibhu [00:51:19]: Like, right now it’s cutting or opening a fridge. Is there. Like, do you set yourself to by this timeline, we should, to stay on track, be able to do whatever?

Jason Ma [00:51:29]: I think, in terms of deployments, we’re exploring many different industries. There isn’t a particular task we think we have to nail, right? Because our goal is to build a general model, a general platform, and we think of each different task as validation of our platform as a way, as a wedge for us to figure out how to build everything better. So today, we are doing a lot of that in laundry, in restaurants. We have already deployed tens of robots, but our goal next year is overall just deploying hundreds of robots.

Vibhu [00:52:02]: My part two on the last technical question is, how do you see the rest of the industry? So fill in for people, what other approaches are people taking to world models? Why are they wrong? What is different but good about their approaches as well? Just what is the landscape of robotic world models in this space and why— how have you come to your current?

Jason Ma [00:52:25]: No, that’s a great question. So I think robotics is the most exciting space today, and there are just so many, amazing companies that I truly respect. They’ve been doing great frontier work like us, and it’s very exciting. And I think what we are seeing today is that there’s still many different approaches to robotics. Like, we believe that hardware needs to be built in-house. We need to own the whole, chain. We believe that scaling human data is extremely important. But there are companies that’s betting on just scaling robots’ data or scaling some sort of intermediate data collection devices, right? All of them are in play, and I think it’s different approaches. We’ll just see what happens. I think right now, it’s still a bit early to tell, but we feel pretty good about the way we’re building things just because we as a company, culture-wise, mission-wise, we’re not here to just build a model. We’re here to truly get robots deployed. So we deploy as much as possible, work on the hard problems. So we identify problems much earlier on. So then I think that really helps us identify what the true bottlenecks are and then solve them. And I think for folks, for people who are only working on one part of the problem, it’s kind of like fog of war. You don’t really see the whole picture, and you might be building something that’s extremely cool technologically, but may not be what people need or want at the end, right? I think there’s a whole graveyard of robotics company, and I think all of them had very shiny, very cool robots, but just figuring out what people actually want is actually. It’s very easy to say “Build something people want.” everyone says that but it’s actually really hard to execute a robotics company.

World Action Models vs. Vision-Language-Action Models

Vibhu [00:54:07]: On the technical side, you have your world action model. Is that standard across industry? Is there other directions people are taking?

Jason Ma [00:54:15]: Yeah, I would say that’s also not standard. So we’re building world action model on top of world model. So there is many companies building world model. You mentioned Runway. They’re also getting to adapt-

Vibhu [00:54:26]: Video world models.

Jason Ma [00:54:27]: There are also companies building a vision language action model.

Vibhu [00:54:31]: VLA.

Jason Ma [00:54:31]: So that’s like taking vision language models and adapting them to robotics. So I think there’s many different ways to go about it. But I think at the end of the day what we call the models is less important than what we believe the model needs to be able to do at a first principle level. So I wanna explain that a bit. I think for robotics, the most important thing is that you need to be able to predict the future. Right. Like robotics, any physical system is fundamentally about based on the information you have at the present moment and before, what should you do next? So it’s really about predicting what comes next. So predicting robot actions is like predicting what the robot should do next. But if you think about it, robot is just a part of the world, right? Robot influences the world, but the world also influences how the robot should behave in that environment. So if you think about it this way, then the maximal, the most first principle thing you can do is just predict as much of the world that you can possibly predict, right? So that’s why we believe predicting the future is extremely important. And today, the instantiation is world action model. And VLA only predicts robot actions or some more abstract representation of the world. But whenever you’re predicting abstract representation of the world, you’re encoding your own bias into what’s important to predict. And the bigger lesson tells you, let’s remove human biases. Let’s just take the most raw representation, the camera inputs, and just predict all of that right? So that’s how I think about, modeling for robotics today.

Swyx [00:56:12]: So just to press you a little bit on this you’re, basically you’re saying your approach is better than the VLA, right? Because you’re emphasizing prediction. I fully buy that. I— Like, you’ve sold me on it. If you were wrong, what is the most likely number two-

Beyond Vision: Tactile, Audio, and Infrared Sensing

Swyx [00:56:26]: Someone else is doing?

Vibhu [00:56:27]: Interesting question.

Jason Ma [00:56:28]: So yeah, there’s a caveat in what I’ve said before, and I think that’s where I could be wrong, right? I said that you need to predict the world as much as possible, right? But what that doesn’t say is that does your sensor have everything about the world that you need to predict? I think I touched on this a little bit, right? Like, if you’re training a world model that’s purely based on videos, I think it will be a very powerful world model, but it may not be a sufficiently rich enough world model because you’re missing critical aspects of the world, like sound, like touch, right? So I think where we could be wrong is like, okay, I have the best world model on vision-based world model, but tomorrow someone else comes out with a vision plus tactile world model that’s just like a hundred X more data efficient just because, vision is a very high information or a highly redundant, input because, every other pixel, they don’t change that much. You can see— you can understand the world without perfect vision. But tactile, other modality might be much denser in information, right? So maybe having that predicting that would just allow you to use much less vision. So you can get to the same performance with much less compute, with much less data, right? But-

Swyx [00:57:51]: I think you will be able to adapt very easily.

Jason Ma [00:57:53]: No, exactly.

Vibhu [00:57:53]: There’s also a level of how much data.

Jason Ma [00:57:56]: Right. So the reason why I bring this up is because I think if a vision-tactile world model or vision-tactile-audio, whatever world model, is the final thing that solves robotics, then I think robotics companies will be able to do that better than video generation companies that’s trying to pivot to robotics. The reason is to understand sensing is actually very complicated. Like, we’ve been building that since the company started, so we know the bottleneck. We know how to combine them. But for— if you’re just trying to adapt a video model to robotics action, then if we were wrong, if, video model is not enough, then you don’t really have the know-how to get tactile to work very well. But we have that.

Swyx [00:58:39]: This is a side question, but I think it’s a quick one. Heat seems very important. Is infrared just another color to you, or is that a.

Jason Ma [00:58:47]: Yeah, it could be another-

Swyx [00:58:48]: Just another color.

Jason Ma [00:58:48]: It could be another color, another input to the model. Could be used in cooking scenario, actually. Like, I know companies that’s using infrared to know how cooked food is. Because that’s really hard to tell from RGB camera, right?

Vibhu [00:59:01]: My very naive pushback on your last point is maybe we don’t need to understand hardware, cloud code, or Codex can just, vibe code it in. There’s a lot you can do without understanding, but of course-

Swyx [00:59:15]: It’s just not in the distribution.

Jason Ma’s Journey: AlphaGo, Penn, NVIDIA, DeepMind, and Dyna

Swyx [00:59:16]: So I wanted to bring it a little bit to your personal story or your background. We both went to Penn.

Jason Ma [00:59:24]: I just found out today. Crazy.

Swyx [00:59:26]: Yes. I, my big regret is I didn’t join the self-drive, the Docker challenge. Which, and then I could have been early Waymo or something. You were at Grasp. And then you’ve also worked at Google and NVIDIA. What are the different focuses of let’s say, academia versus Google versus NVIDIA? You’ve seen all these places, right? And then that obviously caused you to say “Screw all that. I’m gonna do my own thing,” right? You could have joined OpenAI’s robotics lab. So may-just take us through chronologically, but also one thing you learned from each.

Jason Ma [00:59:58]: So chronologically, yeah, maybe it’s useful to talk about how I got into AI in the beginning, right? So, as a kid, so I spent time in Japan and China. I grew up playing Go, the Go in AlphaGo. So when AlphaGo came out, I was a senior in high school, and I was mind-blown because I’ve been playing this game for many years. It’s so complicated. Like, I think before AlphaGo came out, people were like, “Okay, Go is one of the game that AI will never solve.” The search space is larger than the total number of atoms in the world. How could you possibly search for solutions in that? Then RL, reinforcement learning just cracked it, right? And I think that was how I got into AI initially. Like, I was just really interested in models or systems, agents that can self-improve, right? So when I got to Penn as a PhD student, I just really wanted to work on reinforcement learning. So I’m co-advised. Both my advisors were interested in RL at the time. One of my advisor was more in robotics. He did a postdoc at Berkeley Robotics Lab. So that’s how I got into robots. At Penn, we have GRASP Lab, I think one of the best places to do robotics. And so that’s how I got into doing RL for robotics in my PhD. And then, yeah, I did a bunch of research thinking about how to connect reinforcement learning, with human data, how to do reinforcement learning, theory in a very rigorous way. And then I went to NVIDIA. That’s when GPT-4 came out. At the time, we were very interested in just solving a pen spinning task. I don’t know why. Like, -

Swyx [01:01:35]: It’s the dexter- it’s the dexterity limit, right? That you can solve Rubik’s cubes, and then you-

Jason Ma [01:01:39]: At the time, I was working with, -

Swyx [01:01:41]: Jinpeng

Jason Ma [01:01:41]: … Jinpeng at UCO, which you guys probably also know. Like, yeah, we were just like, “Okay, let’s try to do dexterous pen spinning.” The initial idea was learning it from human videos, right? We were trying to watch humans do it. But then I realized, okay, today we don’t have a dexterous hand that can spin pencil at all. So how would I even be able to evaluate the algorithm, even if learning from human worked at all? So I thought, “Okay, we need to first try this in simulation.” Then as soon as I tried to set up a simulated environment for a robot hand with a pen, I immediately saw what the issue is. The issue is like, if I had to come up with this simulation environment, the reward function for reinforcement learning to solve pen spinning, that’s impossible. Like, I wouldn’t be able to come up with all the terms that you need to get RL to learn the right behavior. And then I was just thinking, “What if a model that can write code can do that?” That’s what became the Eureka project, right? We basically. Like, in my opinion, we had the first recursive self-improving robotic agent in simulation, ‘cause we really used that to solve a new task that no one has demonstrated before. And that allowed me to see the potential of using language model, using coding models to really accelerate robotics. So then I went to Google DeepMind, ‘cause at the time, even today, they have one of the frontier models in Gemini, right? So I was looking at how to use Gemini for robotics. But eventually I realized like, I had a lot of fun doing academic research, but there was always a question in the back of my mind “Does any of this matter?” like, when you’re working on this kind of thing in a lab you ask me, “How do we come up with so many interesting, fun tasks?” You’re basically doing your own eval. You’re grading your own homework. Like, I wanted something more real. I wanted something that could actually be used by millions of people in the world. And I felt twenty-twenty-four was when we started Dyna, like end of twenty-twenty-four. That was the right time that we can take some of these technology to actually putting them out in the real world. So that’s why

Jason Ma [01:03:45]: I started Dyna with Lindon Gao and York Yang. And fast-forward two years, we built our platform, our model. Our robots are in Din Tai Fung. Go check it out and, -

Vibhu [01:03:55]: Go eat.

Jason Ma [01:03:56]: Yeah, go eat. It’s been a journey. And,. But what still gets me really excited is, like some of— a lot of the ideas that I temporarily abandoned when we started Dyna, because, to build a company, you have to be very practical. Like, I think simulation wasn’t ready in twenty-twenty-four. But now with like the new frontier models and what we’re seeing internally this might change. And that’s very exciting.

Product-Led Research, Experimental Evals, and Company Culture

Swyx [01:04:20]: And so then also let’s talk about company culture. What principles you’re building the company with. Obviously the— you’re responsible for the science and the research, agenda. And it just seems like when we meet the engineers, they are, they’re very engaged and then they have a lot of ownership. They have a lot of motivations.

Vibhu [01:04:38]: I’ll say it’s interesting to see how many side projects people just work on. So some of the demos we’ve seen, it’s just the engineers that work on it were like “Yeah, this seems fun. Might as well do it.” To your point on fun evals, right here, like two feet behind the camera-

Swyx [01:04:55]: Can’t talk about that.

Vibhu [01:04:57]: … just the e— the eval is just there’s highlighters, four highlighters being rubber banded together, right? It’s like, who comes up with, “ yes, we need to test putting rubber bands on high.” It’s just-

Swyx [01:05:07]: Fissionary-ish

Vibhu [01:05:08]: … fun stuff. People are very … creative here. It’s a beautiful space.

Jason Ma [01:05:12]: Yeah, I think culture. Yeah, so let’s first talk about, how we run a company, right? Like, we think of ourself as like a like a eventually like a research plus product company. It’s kind of like OpenAI where you do frontier research, but eventually all of them make their way into Codex through ChatGPT. That’s how we think about it too. We’re not here to just do open-ended whatever thing that interests us at the time. We’re always product-driven. Like, we wanna deploy our robots, our platform to a new customer. What are the technical problems we have to solve, right? We have to solve generalization. We have to solve whole body control. We have to solve how to adapt quickly. We have to solve how to make the robots follow language. We have to solve dexterity. So once all those problems are very clear, then, like. Our engineers are very capable. They’re very smart. So they just create instances of the task. They create tasks that will stress test those capabilities, right? Like the j— the grabbing a drink task is just how we test language following, right? You can just specify what you want. If the model follows intent, follows instruction, it should be able to do it. So that’s how we think about, like. At the top level, we identify what are the things we have to solve. Then we have a lot of bottom sub-project to actually drive execution to solve them. And you hire the right people. And everyone here is super passionate about robots. They’ve been doing this for a long time. They love it. And we just create a culture where it just naturally happens. And it’s a really fun place to work.

The Team: Hardware, Software, Research, and Learning

Vibhu [01:06:44]: What’s the split between technical research software versus hardware side of the company?

Jason Ma [01:06:51]: We recently grew so much, so I don’t have the perfect number. But I would say on the hardware side, we have, I would say probably like thirty percent, forty percent of hardware, just because hardware you need a lot more people. And then we have around ten people working on models. And then we have software engineers, robotics engineer. We have a lot of very talented people on the business side. The most fun thing about building a robotics company is you see everything. Everything under the sun that could possibly be helpful will be helpful, right? And so you just get so much exposure working with so many different people from many different backgrounds who are all very passionate about robots. And I think it’s been really eye-opening for me as a founder. ‘Cause when I was a researcher at a lab or a PhD student, I was talking to researchers every day, and that was great. That was really good. I still get to do that every day, but now I also get to learn just from so many different people from different walks of life. Like, some of our people who collect data, they had no robotics experience. They were working in retail, working in some other jobs, and they came here, you know. They also became very well-trained in robotics, and I think that’s just pretty amazing to see. And I think of myself as I’m still learning, you know. I think of myself as just always learning in the robotics space, and I haven’t learned so much as I am now. Even though, you think about me now, I’m not a student anymore. I’m here running a company, managing a lot of things, but I still feel like the day-to-day learning is just so much.

Dyna’s Vision and the Origin of Its Name

Swyx [01:08:29]: And then just to close off, where’s Dyna going? Two years, five years, what’s, the vision?

Jason Ma [01:08:37]: Yeah, I think our vision is to truly— The high-level mission is truly bring robots and intelligence, right, into the physical world. Like, actua— That means actually seeing our robots deployed thousands of customers, even more, millions of robots. That’s where we wanna get to.

Vibhu [01:08:58]: What’s the what’s the name from Dyna? Dynamic? Is there a is there a story?

Jason Ma [01:09:03]: Yeah, there’s many stories. So I na— I named Dyna. There were a lot of internal options.

Vibhu [01:09:09]: Take the credit.

Jason Ma [01:09:11]: … internal, different options. But how the name came to be was, there are two things. One is so, Turing Award winner, Richard Sutton, who was the pioneer of reinforcement learning, wrote a paper called Dyna many years ago. It’s about basically an agent that self-improves, world model. And I felt even when we started the company we weren’t doing world model yet, but I felt that’s how robotics will get solved. And now our technology direction is converging to that. So I felt that was a really neat inspiration, also because I worked in reinforcement learning, I have a lot of respect for Richard. The second thing is that it’s a bit more personal. Like, I grew up in Japan, and the year I was born, there was just a cartoon show. I don’t know if you guys have seen Ultraman.

Swyx [01:10:00]: Yeah, of course.

Jason Ma [01:10:01]: The yeah, the Ultraman that year was called Dyna. So, yeah, it’s a very subtle thing not people know, but I guess now everyone would-

Vibhu [01:10:10]: The team is finding out too.

Swyx [01:10:13]: But I think Richard would appreciate it. I don’t know if you ever talked to him, but-

Jason Ma [01:10:16]: No, I’ve seen him at RL conferences.

Swyx [01:10:18]: You should just be like, “Hey, this company-”

Jason Ma [01:10:20]: Yeah, I’ll invite him, come-

Swyx [01:10:21]: Inspired by you.

Vibhu [01:10:22]: Everyone knows Richard for a better lesson, but you know.

Jason Ma [01:10:24]: Yeah, also better lesson.

Swyx [01:10:27]: Okay, any parting thoughts or calls to action?

Closing: Deploying Real Robots and Building the Future

Jason Ma [01:10:31]: Calls to action. Yeah, I think I do feel like as an industry, robotics is still very demo-oriented. Like, I have done a lot of demos in the past in the lab, even here we had to show some demos. But I think we need more people that’s truly, mission-focused on doing whatever it takes to get robots deployed, get, robotic foundation models truly integrated with hardware and seeing them at real customer sites. I think we’re a pioneer on this regard, and I wanna see more in this field. And for the audience that’s watching, if this mission inspires you, if, solving the hardest problems today is what makes you wake up every day and you wanna contribute, we’re always hiring and yeah, looking forward to that.

Swyx [01:11:14]: Bay Area? Anywhere else?

Jason Ma [01:11:16]: Yes, just Bay Area today.

Swyx [01:11:18]: Bay Area.

Jason Ma [01:11:18]: But as company grows, never say never to other locations. Yeah, but that’s what I wanna say, and I wanted to see more robots in the world.

Swyx [01:11:27]: Cool. Congrats on everything. This is incredible progress for two years. Yeah. Amazing.

Jason Ma [01:11:34]: Yeah, I really appreciate it. Thank you for visiting us. I hope it’s been fun.

Swyx [01:11:40]: I don’t regret doing this on site. We do a lot of interviews in our studio, but this was worth it.

Jason Ma [01:11:48]: I think for robotics, gotta do it on site.

Vibhu [01:11:51]: For people listening in, watch the video version. We have fun B-roll.

author: agrawal-aka

raw.title: viable/strict/1791906918: [AARCH64] Use oneDNN jit:int8 matmul for torch._int_mm (#200389)
raw.author: agrawal-aka
raw.content:
On AArch64, torch._int_mm always uses the native fallback loop. TorchAO's Int8DynamicActivationInt8WeightConfig calls _int_mm on CPU, so int8 linear layers don't benefit from oneDNN.

Since v3.13, oneDNN's AArch64 jit:int8 matmul (SVE + I8MM) supports s32 output (uxlfoundation/oneDNN#5267). This PR routes _int_mm to it.

Changes (AArch64 only; x86 unchanged)

  • Dispatch _int_mm to oneDNN when the CPU has SVE and I8MM.

  • Let oneDNN choose the weight layout (format_tag::any) and make src contiguous. jit:int8 rejects fixed transposed weights and non-row-major src; without this, oneDNN falls back to gemm:jit, which runs the reference gemm.

  • No new ops or API changes. This supersedes the approach in #180455.

Performance Impact:
torch._int_mm per-call latency (ms)

  • Machine: AWS Graviton3E, 32 cores
  • Before: 2.16.0a0+git8ab9c86
  • After: 2.16.0a0+git66b13a3

N = 4096, K = 4096

M Before After
1 0.2384 0.3076
4 0.9043 0.3081
8 1.7937 0.3091
16 3.5728 0.3267
32 7.0981 0.3663
64 14.2603 0.4053
128 28.4878 0.5561
256 56.7760 0.7947

N = 4096, K = 11008

M Before After
1 0.6199 0.9591
4 2.4000 0.8683
8 4.7804 0.8548
16 9.5277 0.9677
32 19.1414 1.0404
64 38.2573 1.2001
128 76.2403 1.4724
256 152.0425 2.1462

Test script :

import torch
import time
import torch.profiler as profiler

torch.manual_seed(0)

print("Torch version:", torch.__version__)

# Fixed dimensions
K, N = 4096, 4096
# K, N = 4096, 11008

# Sweep M
M_values = [1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]

# Number of iterations
WARMUP = 10
ITERS = 100

print("\n=== Per-call latency (ms) ===")
print(f"{'M':>6} | {'Latency (ms)':>15}")
print("-" * 28)

for M in M_values:
    # Create tensors
    A = torch.randint(-128, 127, (M, K), dtype=torch.int8)
    B = torch.randint(-128, 127, (N, K), dtype=torch.int8)

    # Warmup
    for _ in range(WARMUP):
        torch._int_mm(A, B.t())

    # Timing
    start = time.time()
    for _ in range(ITERS):
        C = torch._int_mm(A, B.t())
    end = time.time()

    latency_ms = (end - start) * 1000 / ITERS
    print(f"{M:6d} | {latency_ms:15.4f}")

Tests :
Passes already existing tests for int_mm:
python test/test_linalg.py -k test__int_mm_cpu -v

author: adabeyta

raw.title: viable/strict/1791923525:  [Stable-ABI] Move acc_type into torch::headeronly. (#199203)
raw.author: adabeyta
raw.content:
Moves the accumulate-type traits into torch::headeronly. Needed for torchvision stable-ABI, which currently carries a local AccType helper that only covers the types it dispatches.

Summary

  • Introduces acc_type, acc_type_device, AccumulateType and AccumulateTypeDevice in the torch::headeronly namespace.

BC-breaking note

at::AccumulateTypeDevice can no longer be specialized inside namespace at

Moves the trait definition to torch::headeronly so at::AccumulateTypeDevice is now a using declaration. Code that specializes it inside namespace at no longer compiles.

Previously a specialization compiled and at::acc_type returned the type it named. To get the previous behavior, specialize in torch::headeronly instead.

Example (the same applies to at::AccumulateType) :

Version 2.14.0:

namespace at {
template <>
struct AccumulateTypeDevice<MyType, c10::DeviceType::CPU> {
  using type = double;
};
}

Version 2.15.0:

// The code above fails with:
// error: specialization of 'template<class T, c10::DeviceType D> struct torch::headeronly::AccumulateTypeDevice' in different namespace

// Specialize it by its torch::headeronly name:
template <>
struct torch::headeronly::AccumulateTypeDevice<MyType, c10::DeviceType::CPU> {
  using type = double;
};

Pull Request resolved: #199203
Approved by: https://github.com/janeyx99

title: viable/strict/1791919581: [MPS] Fix precision loss in complex sqrt (#200736)
summary: The Metal complex sqrt computed the imaginary part as sqrt((|z| - re) / 2), which suffers catastrophic cancellation when |im| << re (and the real part likewise via |z| + re when re < 0). E.g. on MPS sqrt(1+1e-4j) returned 1+0j instead of 1+5e-5j for complex64, and chalf sqrt(0.7783+0.0038j) had a 3.4x error in the imaginary part, which made test_sqrt fail once its explicit seed was removed. Fix by adding a c10::metal::sqrt overload for complex types that computes the larger component as sqrt((|re| + |z|) / 2) and derives the other one by division (computed in float, using hypot for the modulus
author: malfet

The Metal complex sqrt computed the imaginary part as sqrt((|z| - re) / 2), which suffers catastrophic cancellation when |im| << re (and the real part likewise via |z| + re when re < 0). E.g. on MPS sqrt(1+1e-4j) returned 1+0j instead of 1+5e-5j for complex64, and chalf sqrt(0.7783+0.0038j) had a 3.4x error in the imaginary part, which made test_sqrt fail once its explicit seed was removed.

The scalar-shaped iterator only configures the output; the reduction implementation builds its own normally shaped iterator for the calculation.

All 16 current storage regression cases pass, covering both reductions, matching and mixed dtypes, and scalar or empty out= tensors. The original matching-dtype and native out= regression cases were recorded failing on the unpatched checkout before the fix. Selected repository suites passed 97 tests with 41 skips, including loss, operator, module, metadata, and forward/reverse gradient tests. Spin lint passed. [# Web Development: A Complete Guide for Beginner

https://e-laeltd.com/

Introduction

In today's digital world, having a website is essential for businesses, organizations, and individuals. Websites help businesses showcase their products, connect with customers, and build a strong online presence. Web development plays an important role in creating these websites.

Whether you want to become a professional web developer, start freelancing, or build your own website, learning web development can open up many exciting opportunities.

What Is Web Development?

https://e-laeltd.com/

Web development is the process of creating, building, and maintaining websites and web applications. It includes designing website layouts, writing code, managing databases, and ensuring that websites work properly across different devices.

Web development generally involves three main areas: front-end development, back-end development, and full-stack development.

Types of Web Development

1. Front-End Development

Front-end development focuses on the parts of a website that users see and interact with. It includes website layouts, navigation menus, buttons, forms, images, and animations.

The main technologies used in front-end development are:

  • HTML: Defines the structure of a webpage.
  • CSS: Controls the design, colors, layout, and appearance.
  • JavaScript: Adds interactivity and dynamic behavior.

Front-end developers work to make websites attractive, responsive, and easy to use.

https://e-laeltd.com/

2. Back-End Development

Back-end development focuses on the server-side functionality of a website. It manages data, user authentication, business logic, and communication between the server and the front end.

Popular back-end technologies include:

  • Node.js
  • Python
  • PHP
  • Java
  • SQL databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL

Back-end development helps ensure that websites function securely and efficiently.

3. Full-Stack Development

Full-stack development combines front-end and back-end development. Full-stack developers can work on the user interface, server-side logic, databases, and integration between different parts of a web application.

Learning full-stack development can be useful for people who want to understand how an entire website works.

Why Is Web Development Important?

Web development offers many benefits for individuals and businesses.

  • Online Presence: Helps businesses reach customers through the internet.
  • Business Growth: Supports product promotion, online sales, and customer communication.
  • Better User Experience: Makes websites easier to navigate and use.
  • Automation: Enables online forms, booking systems, dashboards, and other useful features.
  • Career Opportunities: Creates opportunities for employment, freelancing, and entrepreneurship.

Essential Skills for Web Developers

If you want to become a web developer, start by developing these essential skills:

HTML and CSS

Learn how to structure webpages with HTML and style them using CSS. These are the foundations of front-end development.

JavaScript

JavaScript helps you build interactive features such as dropdown menus, form validation, dynamic content, and interactive web applications.

Responsive Web Design

https://e-laeltd.com/

Responsive design ensures that websites work well on desktops, tablets, and smartphones.

Git and GitHub

Git helps developers track changes in their code, while GitHub provides a platform for hosting repositories and collaborating with other developers.

Database Fundamentals

Learn how databases store, organize, and retrieve information. Database knowledge is particularly important for back-end and full-stack development.

Problem-Solving

Web developers need to identify bugs, understand errors, and find practical solutions to technical problems.

How to Start Learning Web Development

Follow these steps if you are a beginner:

  1. Learn HTML and create a simple webpage.
  2. Study CSS to improve the design and layout.
  3. Learn JavaScript to add interactive features.
  4. Build small projects, such as a personal portfolio or calculator.
  5. Learn Git and GitHub to manage and showcase your code.
  6. Explore a front-end framework or a back-end technology after learning the fundamentals.
  7. Create a portfolio website to display your projects.
  8. Practise regularly and apply for internships, jobs, or freelance projects.

Best Tools for Web Development

Several tools can make web development easier and more efficient.

  • Visual Studio Code: A popular code editor.
  • Google Chrome DevTools: Helps inspect webpages and debug code.
  • Git: Tracks changes in source code.
  • GitHub: Hosts code and supports collaboration.
  • Figma: Helps with interface design and prototyping.
  • Vite: A development tool for building modern web projects.

Beginners do not need to learn every tool at once. Start with a code editor, a browser, and the basic web technologies.

Career Opportunities in Web Development

Web development offers several career paths, including:

  • Front-End Developer
  • Back-End Developer
  • Full-Stack Developer
  • WordPress Developer
  • Web Application Developer
  • Freelance Web Developer

Your opportunities will depend on your skills, portfolio, practical experience, and ability to solve real-world problems.

Common Mistakes Beginners Should Avoid

Many beginners try to learn too many programming languages at once. This can make the learning process confusing.

Other common mistakes include copying code without understanding it, avoiding practical projects, ignoring responsive design, and giving up when errors appear.

Instead, focus on one topic at a time, practise consistently, and build projects that demonstrate your abilities.

The Future of Web Development

Web development continues to evolve with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, modern JavaScript frameworks, improved web security, and progressive web applications.

Developers who keep learning, understand web fundamentals, and adapt to new technologies can remain better prepared for changes in the industry.

Conclusion

Web development is a valuable skill that allows you to create websites and powerful web applications. By learning HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and the fundamentals of back-end development, beginners can build a strong foundation for a career in technology.

The most effective way to learn web development is through consistent practice and real-world projects.

Start learning web development today and take your first step toward building your own website and a successful career in technology!

raw.title: Open weights in production: five builder takeaways from Chain of Thought
raw.dc:creator: Conor Bronsdon
raw.content:
Open weights are easy to cheer for and hard to run profitably. The questions that decide it are what you pay per task, what you must prove to a customer, and how much of the system lives outside the weights. A leaderboard alone cannot settle them. Below is one practical takeaway per episode from the Chain of Thought collection on open source AI. (To follow new episodes on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify or by email, use the subscribe page.)

What changed the week DeepSeek R1 landed?

When DeepSeek changed the AI race overnight, the argument on the show was recorded while the news was still settling. That timing matters for builders: treat the episode as a snapshot of how people were reframing cost and openness.

The practical read is the price floor. DeepSeek's R1 release forced a rethink of what an open model was allowed to cost and what that implies for how models get built next. Export controls and "Agents as a Service" came up as second-order questions, but the builder move is simpler. Re-run your inference budget assumptions and your roadmap for agentic features, because the conversation also tied heavier agent stacks to the need for serious evaluation of agent behavior beyond single-turn demos.

If you are adding tools, memory, or multi-step flows, plan how you will measure agent performance before you scale traffic. The episode pairs the shock of R1 with agentic evaluation as the guardrail layer that complexity demands.

When does one summarization bill justify fine-tuning Qwen?

How Intercom cut $250K/month by ditching GPT for open models is the most concrete open-weights-in-production walkthrough on the show. Intercom was spending $250K a month on a single summarization task on GPT, then moved to a fine-tuned 14B Qwen model and saved almost all of that spend.

Do not copy "swap model, save money" without copying the surrounding system. Fergal Reid's story for Fin is that resolution moved from about 30% to nearly 70%, and most of that lift came from custom re-rankers, retrieval models, and query canonicalization rather than from swapping the core frontier LLM alone. Benchmarks can lie in production (Goodhart's law shows up explicitly in the episode), so Intercom leaned on A/B tests with soft versus hard resolution definitions.

Decision rule I'd steal: isolate the task with a brutal monthly line item, then ask whether a smaller open model plus fine-tuning beats API spend. If the task is narrow (summarization, canonicalization), run production tests beyond benchmarks before you commit. Remember the latency wrinkle Reid describes: slower responses can raise resolution rates, which breaks the instinct to optimize only for speed.

What does an open ecosystem bet mean if you are not picking the GPU?

AMD's challenge to NVIDIA: the open ecosystem bet is hardware-heavy, but the builder lesson is lock-in. Anush Elangovan frames AMD's MI350 series on CDNA 4 architecture, including 20 petaflops of FP4 performance he calls mind blowing, as part of a full-stack push paired with ROCm 7 and AMD Developer Cloud with Day Zero support for frontier models.

Sharon Zhou's half of the conversation is about making contribution real: a happy path for community work, teaching, and listening to developers and treating open source as more than a press release. For application teams, the takeaway is to know your escape hatches. If training or serving depends on one vendor's CUDA-only path, your open-model strategy can still die on infrastructure bills or portability. Ask whether your stack has a credible second home before you bake in assumptions.

How should you ship an on-machine open agent without ignoring safety?

AI, open source, and developer safety with Block's Rizel Scarlett centers on Goose, Block's on-machine open source agent built to automate engineering work, including starting with migrations for Block employees. Block also collaborated with Anthropic on MCPs, which is a reminder, in my reading, that open agents still sit in an ecosystem of other people's work. What it gives you is the ability to inspect and adapt more of the stack.

Rizel Scarlett ties open source agent tooling to developer safety, including psychological safety for junior developers, plus responsible and ethical use and community involvement when building developer tools. Practical procedure: default sensitive work to on-machine agents where policy allows, document what the agent can touch, and treat openness as a reason to involve the community in review while keeping your guardrails.

What should enterprises weigh before open versus proprietary?

The state of AI: open-source models and enterprise trust was the show's first episode, and it frames open versus proprietary as an enterprise trust question more than a benchmark contest. Writer CEO May Habib talks about implementing generative AI at scale and the challenges of productionizing GenAI.

I'd start checklists with trust artifacts before parameter counts: who is liable for output, how humans stay in the loop, and what breaks in deployment that demos never saw. Regulation and election-era policy show up in the episode framing, but the builder question I take from her segment is whether your customer can rely on the system in production, open weights or not.

Optional sketch for comparing paths on one task (illustration only, not Intercom's pipeline):

# Sketch: per-task economics + trust gates (not production code)
def should_explore_open_weights(task):
    gates = {
        "monthly_api_spend": task.api_usd_per_month,  # e.g. one bad summarization line item
        "task_narrow": task.is_single_purpose,
        "eval_in_prod": task.has_ab_not_only_benchmarks,
        "trust_requirements": task.enterprise_checklist_done,
    }
    return gates["monthly_api_spend"] > 0 and gates["eval_in_prod"]

Checklist

  • Re-budget inference after open-model price shocks (R1-scale events) and add agent evals before you scale tool-using flows.
  • For high-spend single tasks, model Intercom's pattern: fine-tuned open weights plus retrieval, re-ranking, and canonicalization, with production A/B tests instead of leaderboard faith.
  • Map hardware and software lock-in (CUDA-only paths vs open stack options like ROCm and developer cloud Day Zero support) before you commit training pipelines.
  • Ship open agents like Goose with clear on-machine boundaries, MCP integrations where needed, and explicit safety practices for junior-heavy teams.
  • For enterprise buyers, lead with trust and productionization lessons (the episode's framing) before open source ideology.

More on this topic, with the related episodes, is on Chain of Thought. It draws on this episode.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.

title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
summary: Learn how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory and Anchor Browser built AI agents that autonomously pay for x402-protected web resources and APIs. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments checks budgets, signs transactions, and retries requests without exposing wallet credentials to the agent runtime.
author: Cher Simon

raw.creator: Cher Simon
raw.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
raw.content:encoded:
AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention.

Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory, it’s now available on AWS Marketplace. This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction.

Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch.

When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption.

Challenges

When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention.

Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity:

Payment protocol handling

  • Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors.
  • Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects.
  • Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent.
  • Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.

Security and key management

  • Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs.
  • Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.

Operational resilience

  • Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.
  • Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations.
  • Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.

Observability and compliance

  • Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.

Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including:

  • Signing the proof.
  • Attaching the correct header.
  • Retrying the request.
  • Settling the transaction.
  • Logging the result.

Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward.

Figure 1: Agent payment stack

The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.

Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.

Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.

Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.

Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed.

Solution

Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure.

Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. --url https://api.anchorbrowser.io/v1/sessions

    'content-type': 'application/json',

The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort.

Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs.

Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds.

Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place.

Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed.

Solution

Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure.

Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows.

AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure:

  • A PaymentConnector integrates the Payment Manager with an external wallet provider, either Coinbase Developer Platform (Coinbase CDP) or Stripe Privy.
  • A PaymentCredentialProvider stores wallet provider credentials securely in AgentCore Identity.
  • A PaymentInstrument identifies the specific wallet address from which funds are drawn.

Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, so agents can discover available pay-per-use x402 endpoints programmatically.

AgentCore payments restructures the payment architecture. Sensitive operations move out of the agent runtime and into a managed service layer. The Anchor Agent holds only two payment-related components: a budget session and the x402 tool. The infrastructure, including authentication, wallet secrets, payment limits, observability, and payment proof signing, resides in the AgentCore payments layer. Figure 2 shows the Anchor Agent connecting to the AgentCore payments managed layer, which handles wallet provider integration with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy.

Figure 2: Anchor Browser integrates with AgentCore payments

How the payment flow works

The following steps describe what happens end to end, from the moment a browser session encounters an x402-protected resource to the moment the agent receives the response and continues the task.

  1. Anchor Browser creates a dedicated AgentCore PaymentSession for the browser session. When the session starts with x402 turned on, Anchor Browser provisions a PaymentSession through AgentCore payments, linking the browser session to a configured payment instrument and budget.
  2. The browser receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent navigates to a URL or makes a fetch or XMLHttpRequest (XHR) request. The merchant responds with a 402 challenge specifying the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address.
  3. The browser selects a compatible payment method. Anchor Browser reads the 402 challenge payload and matches the requested payment method against the instrument linked to the PaymentSession.
  4. AgentCore verifies the session budget and generates the cryptographic payment proof. AgentCore payments validates that the payment amount falls within the session spending limit. The service then signs the transaction using the configured wallet provider (Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy) and returns the cryptographic proof. No key material enters the browser or agent runtime.
  5. The browser retries the original request with the payment header. The browser attaches the signed proof as PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2 or X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, then retries the original request exactly once.
  6. The merchant verifies and settles the payment, then returns the protected resource. The merchant validates the cryptographic proof, settles the transaction on-chain, and serves the content. The agent continues the task.

Wallet credentials remain with AgentCore and the configured wallet provider throughout this flow.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure that you have a valid Anchor Browser API key (ANCHOR_API_KEY). To create one, see the Anchor Browser Quick Start guide.

Setting up automatic x402 payments

Setting up agentic payments for Anchor Browser requires one session property. Set session.x402 to true. The property defaults to false. When enabled, the browser session can automatically access x402-protected websites with payments signed by AgentCore payments and retried inside the same browser session. Enabling session.x402 authorizes the browser to make real payments from the configured payment instrument.

The following examples show how to create a payment-enabled session for Anchor Browser using cURL and JavaScript:

cURL

curl --request POST
--url https://api.anchorbrowser.io/v1/sessions
--header "anchor-api-key: $ANCHOR_API_KEY"
--header "content-type: application/json"
--data '{"session":{"x402":true}}'

JavaScript

const response = await fetch('https://api.anchorbrowser.io/v1/sessions', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'anchor-api-key': process.env.ANCHOR_API_KEY,
    'content-type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ session: { x402: true } }),
});
const { data: session } = await response.json();
console.log(session.cdp_url);

After connected through Chrome DevTools Protocol, the agent navigates normally. You don’t need to include a wallet key or payment header in your automation code. The browser handles 402 challenges, payment signing, and retries transparently for document navigation, fetch, and XHR requests.

Payment session limits and behavior

Anchor Browser enforces the following guardrails at the session level through AgentCore payments integration. Each payment-ready browser session operates within configured spending and time constraints. For specific limits, refer to the Anchor Browser technical documentation.

If the merchant response is malformed, no compatible network is offered, the budget is exhausted, or AgentCore payments rejects the payment, the browser returns the original 402 response to the page unchanged. Your automation code can then handle the 402 as a standard HTTP error.

The x402 session property controls payments to third-party resources only. The property doesn’t replace Anchor credits and doesn’t pay for the browser session.

Automation code for Anchor Browser

Your automation code for Anchor Browser remains unchanged. The following example demonstrates that no payment-specific code is required:

const { chromium } = require('playwright');
// Connect to the x402-enabled session via CDP
const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(session.cdp_url);
const page = await browser.newPage();
// Navigate to an x402-protected resource exactly as with a free page
await page.goto('https://premium-research.example.com/market-report');
// The page loaded, the payment was handled automatically
// Extract content as normal
const content = await page.textContent('article');

No wallet logic, no payment header construction, and no retry code. The agent navigates to the URL. If the server returns 402, Anchor Browser coordinates with AgentCore payments to sign the payment proof, retries the request with the appropriate payment header, and delivers the content to the page. Your automation code receives the final rendered page with no indication that a payment occurred.

This pattern applies uniformly to paywalled journalism, licensed financial data, gated API documentation, metered research databases, and other resources that gate content behind a 402 challenge.

Using the built-in x402 tool for API calls

Paid resources aren’t limited to web pages. Many are APIs that expect POST, PUT, or other HTTP methods. Common examples include data enrichment services, premium inference endpoints, and licensed content APIs. For these use cases, Anchor Browser agents include a built-in x402 tool that you call like a standard HTTPS API within the browser context.

Your agent makes the API call through fetch or XHR. If the server returns a 402 challenge, the browser coordinates payment signing through AgentCore payments and retries the request with the signed payment header. Your code receives the response as though the endpoint were free. The tool isn’t tied to a specific vendor, model, or framework. Payment operates as a session-level capability beneath your existing tooling, and no changes to agent code are required.

// Fetch call to a paid API endpoint within the x402-enabled session
const response = await page.evaluate(async () => {
  const res = await fetch('https://data-enrichment.example.com/api/v1/enrich', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ company_domain: 'example.com' }),
  });
  return res.json();
});
// If the API returned 402, AgentCore handled payment automatically
// The response contains the enriched data
console.log(response);

Your automation code doesn’t receive wallet credentials. Automatic payments are available only when session.x402 is set to true and remain subject to the spending and expiration limits described in the previous section.

Key benefits

This integration moves payment from application code to the infrastructure layer:

No payment infrastructure to build. No wallet SDK to integrate, no 402 response parser to write, no retry loop to implement, no header construction logic to maintain, and no custom audit logging to build. AgentCore payments manages the entire payment stack.

No changes to existing tooling. Playwright scripts, Puppeteer automations, Chrome DevTools Protocol commands, and agent flows in Anchor Browser continue to function exactly as before. Payment is a session capability attached to the browser, not a modification to agent logic, prompts, or tool definitions.

Private keys don’t enter the runtime. Signing and settlement happen inside AgentCore payments. The service communicates with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy through secure credential storage in AgentCore Identity. The agent runtime doesn’t have access to key material that can move funds.

Budgets are enforced at the infrastructure level. Every session operates within defined spend limits that AgentCore enforces before authorizing a payment. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability provides full payment audit trails through Amazon CloudWatch. When a session reaches the spending limit, AgentCore payments denies the payment.

Paid tasks complete successfully. Paid GET pages load. Paid API calls return responses. The agent completes the workflow rather than stopping at a 402 response and requiring manual intervention.

Billing is consolidated. Anchor Browser settles third-party x402 charges in credits on the same invoice as browser session time. There’s no separate crypto custody to manage, no USDC balance to monitor, and no on-chain settlement for the finance team to reconcile.

Conclusion

Anchor Browser, integrated with AgentCore payments, equips AI agents to handle x402 payment challenges autonomously for paywalled web pages and paid API endpoints. Wallet credentials stay out of agent code, and no custom payment infrastructure is required.

As more of the web moves to per-request pricing, agents that lack a payment mechanism can’t complete tasks involving paid resources. This integration addresses that gap: agents complete paid workflows end to end, operating within defined budgets, with full observability through AgentCore Observability, and without cryptographic key material in the runtime.

To get started, explore the following resources:

  • Automatic x402 payments in Anchor Browser
  • AgentCore payments developer guide
  • AgentCore payments with browser integration
  • Anchor Browser on AWS Marketplace

About the authors

Cher Simon

Cher is a Principal Deep Learning Architect at AWS, where she helps customers, startups, and AWS Partners build large-scale, high-performance AI/ML solutions. A published author, she specializes in translating AI research into production-ready solutions.

Guy Ben Simhon

Guy is a Co-Founder and CPO at Anchor Browser, leading product and strategy. He focuses on building infrastructure that enables AI agents to reliably interact with the web and operate real computer environments at scale.

Elay Gelbart

Elay is a Founding and Lead Engineer at Anchor Browser, pioneering its browser infrastructure and core engineering. He specializes in large-scale browser infrastructure, distributed systems, and building reliable execution environments for AI agents.

Chethan Shriyan

Chethan is a Principal Product Manager – Technical at AWS. He has more than 12 years of experience in product and business management. Chethan is passionate about building and delivering technology products that create meaningful impact in customers’ lives.

Peter Jiang

Peter is a Senior Software Developer at AWS, based in Seattle, WA. He is a core member of the engineering team behind the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments initiative, which enables payment capabilities for AI agents. With over 8 years of experience in the financial and payments industry, Peter has launched multiple greenfield projects spanning banking, crypto, and agentic systems.

raw.title: I run CrowLLM: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of every major AI provider
raw.dc:creator: Musaw
raw.content:
I'm 18, I built this on my own, and I'll be upfront: this post introduces something I made, and the last line has a link. Everything above it is how it actually works.

Why I built it

I started with one AI provider. Then another had a model I wanted, so I added a second SDK, a second key, a second billing page, and a second rate limit to get stuck behind. Then the first provider had a bad afternoon and my app noticed before I did.

Meanwhile, free users and small builders get treated like an afterthought almost everywhere: slow replies, tiny limits, long waits. A lot of them are students and roleplayers who just want good models without a corporate budget. That's who I built this for.

What it is

One base URL. OpenAI-compatible format. You change the model string, not your code.

curl https://crowllm.com/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CROWLLM_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "write the next line"}]
  }'

The same key works for Claude-family, Gemini-family, GPT-family and DeepSeek models, plus the rest of the catalogue. Streaming works like you'd expect. There's also a /v1/messages endpoint if your client speaks the Anthropic format, including count_tokens.

It works with Cursor, Cline, and the chat front-ends the roleplay community uses, like JanitorAI and SillyTavern. If it speaks the OpenAI format, it should work.

Three kinds of models

Free. Free forever, no card, no trial timer. Sign in with Discord and you can try them right away.

Earned. Play games with the Crow bot in our Discord, bank credit, and spend it on models.

Paid. Pay-as-you-go, token by token. I keep prices as low as I can, below the official provider rates wherever possible, and every rate is printed before you call it, so you can compare with the provider's own page instead of trusting me. I buy my API supply from official, trusted sources.

What's different from calling providers one by one

Failover is real, not a badge. A request that fails upstream is retried on another channel serving the same model. You don't write that loop, and you don't pay twice for it.

Retry cost is on me. If an upstream returns a 429, that failed attempt never shows up on your bill.

Cache reads are priced as cache reads. If a provider discounts cached input, the discount reaches your bill.

No forced IP pinning. A key should work from a train, not only from one machine at home.

Real numbers, publicly readable. The status page at crowllm.com/status only shows real traffic. I'd rather show you a bad week than print a number I made up.

If you're a heavy user, the monthly pass gives you about 5x the credit the same money buys on a top-up, with no request-rate limit.

Where things stand

We're at around +7k users, and we have a friendly community on Discord: discord.gg/crow. The site is still being built. There's no registered company yet, and I'm not planning one until we hit 100k users. :p

What I want from you

Tell me what breaks. If a model behaves differently through the gateway than it does direct, that's a bug and I want the exact request shape. Issues and DMs both work. I'm one person, so I read everything.

crowllm.com — sign in with Discord, try the free models, no card.

Pricing
