raw.title: MissionFlows vs. Workflows: How Adaptive Agent Execution Replaces Static DAGs
raw.dc:creator: mech.app
raw.content:
Traditional workflow engines assume the execution path is known before the first step runs. Airflow DAGs, Temporal workflows, and Prefect pipelines all encode a graph of tasks with edges that represent control flow. When step three fails, you retry step three. When a condition evaluates false, you follow the predefined else branch.

Agentic systems break that assumption. Instead of defining the path, you define a mission and let an LLM-backed agent decide the steps at runtime. If SFTP fails, the agent tries an API. If credentials expire, it refreshes them. If the primary endpoint is down, it selects a fallback. The mission stays constant. The execution path emerges.

This shift creates new infrastructure problems. How do you observe a workflow that writes itself? How do you version control execution logic that lives in prompts instead of YAML? How do you recover from failure when there is no predefined retry branch?

What a Workflow Gives You

A workflow engine provides three guarantees:

  1. Deterministic execution graph. You can visualize the DAG before it runs. Every node and edge is explicit.
  2. Checkpoint boundaries. State is saved at task boundaries. Retry logic is declarative.
  3. Audit trail. You know which tasks ran, in what order, and what they returned.

These guarantees make workflows debuggable. When a pipeline fails, you open the UI, see the red node, inspect the logs, and fix the task. The failure surface is bounded by the DAG structure.

What a MissionFlow Trades Away

A MissionFlow replaces the DAG with a goal and a set of guardrails. The agent receives a mission like "ensure this file reaches the destination securely before 17:00 and verify processing." It does not receive a list of steps.

The agent decides:

  • Which protocol to use (SFTP, API, S3 presigned URL).
  • How to handle credential expiration (refresh token, request new credentials, escalate to human).
  • What constitutes success (file transferred, checksum verified, downstream system acknowledged).

The execution path is not predetermined. It is discovered through reasoning steps that depend on runtime context: API availability, credential validity, network conditions, and the agent's interpretation of the mission.

This introduces three new failure modes:

  1. Reasoning drift. The agent misinterprets the mission and pursues a path that satisfies the literal goal but violates implicit constraints.
  2. Unbounded exploration. Without explicit guardrails, the agent may try dozens of approaches, consuming tokens and time without converging.
  3. Non-reproducible failure. The same mission with the same inputs may produce different execution paths, making debugging harder.

Observability Without a DAG

Traditional workflow UIs render a graph with nodes colored green or red. You see the execution path at a glance. MissionFlows need a different observability model.

Trace Logs of Reasoning Steps

Instead of task boundaries, you log reasoning steps:

{
  "mission_id": "file-transfer-20261013-1847",
  "step": 3,
  "reasoning": "SFTP connection failed with timeout. Checking for alternative endpoints.",
  "action": "query_service_registry",
  "result": "found API endpoint with valid credentials",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-13T18:47:23Z"
}

Each step captures:

  • What the agent observed (SFTP timeout).
  • What it decided (query service registry).
  • What it did (called the registry API).
  • What it learned (found an alternative endpoint).

This log structure replaces the DAG visualization. You reconstruct the execution path by reading the trace.

State Checkpoints Mid-Reasoning

Workflows checkpoint at task boundaries. MissionFlows need to checkpoint mid-reasoning because the agent may decide to pause, request human input, or wait for an external condition.

A checkpoint includes:

  • The mission definition.
  • The reasoning trace so far.
  • The current context (credentials, endpoints, partial results).
  • The agent's next planned action.

If the agent crashes or times out, you can resume from the last checkpoint. The agent re-reads the trace, re-evaluates the context, and continues.

Guardrails as Executable Constraints

Without explicit guardrails, an agent may pursue any path that satisfies the mission. Guardrails are constraints that limit the search space:

  • Allowed tools. The agent can call sftp_transfer, api_upload, and s3_presigned_url, but not ssh_exec.
  • Credential scope. The agent can refresh tokens but cannot request new API keys.
  • Time budget. The agent must complete the mission within 30 minutes or escalate.
  • Approval gates. If the agent wants to use a fallback endpoint not in the approved list, it must request human approval.

Guardrails are enforced by the orchestration layer, not the LLM. The agent proposes actions. The orchestrator checks them against the guardrails before execution.

Failure Recovery Without Predefined Retry Logic

In a workflow, retry logic is declarative:

task: transfer_file
  retry:
    max_attempts: 3
    backoff: exponential

In a MissionFlow, the agent decides whether to retry, try a different approach, or escalate. The orchestrator does not know in advance what "retry" means because the execution path is not fixed.

Agent-Driven Retry

The agent observes a failure, reasons about the cause, and decides the next action:

  • If the failure is transient (network timeout), retry the same action.
  • If the failure is permanent (invalid credentials), try a different approach.
  • If the failure is ambiguous (500 error), inspect logs or query a monitoring system.

The orchestrator logs the agent's reasoning and enforces guardrails, but it does not dictate the recovery strategy.

Escalation Boundaries

When the agent cannot make progress, it escalates. Escalation is a guardrail:

  • If the agent has tried three different approaches and all failed, escalate to a human operator.
  • If the agent needs to use a tool outside the approved list, request approval.
  • If the mission deadline is approaching and the agent is not confident it can complete, escalate early.

Escalation boundaries prevent unbounded exploration. They turn a potentially infinite search into a bounded one with a human in the loop.

Versioning Mission Definitions

Workflows are versioned as code. You commit a YAML file to Git, and the workflow engine executes that version.

MissionFlows are versioned as prompts and guardrails. The mission definition includes:

  • The goal statement (natural language).
  • The guardrails (allowed tools, credential scope, time budget, approval gates).
  • The context schema (what information the agent receives at runtime).

Versioning a mission means versioning the prompt template and the guardrail configuration. Changes to the prompt can change the execution path without changing the code.

Prompt Drift

A workflow DAG is deterministic. The same inputs produce the same execution path. A MissionFlow is not. The same mission with the same inputs may produce different execution paths if the LLM's behavior changes (model update, temperature setting, token budget).

To mitigate prompt drift:

  • Pin the LLM version and parameters.
  • Log the full prompt and response for every reasoning step.
  • Run regression tests that validate the execution path for known scenarios.

Regression tests for MissionFlows are harder than for workflows because the execution path is not fixed. You test outcomes, not paths.

Architecture: Orchestrator, Agent, and Tool Layer

A MissionFlow system has three layers:

Layer Responsibility
Orchestrator Receives the mission, enforces guardrails, logs reasoning steps, manages checkpoints, handles escalation.
Agent Receives the mission and context, reasons about the next action, proposes tool calls, interprets results.
Tool Layer Executes actions (SFTP transfer, API call, database query), returns results to the agent.

The orchestrator is stateful. It maintains the mission state, the reasoning trace, and the checkpoint history. It does not reason. It enforces constraints and logs decisions.

The agent is stateless. It receives the mission, the current context, and the reasoning trace. It returns the next action. The orchestrator decides whether to execute that action based on guardrails.

The tool layer is also stateless. Each tool is a function that takes parameters and returns a result. Tools do not know about missions or agents. They are reusable primitives.

Example: File Transfer Mission 

# Mission definition
mission = {
    "goal": "Transfer file to destination securely before 17:00 and verify processing",
    "guardrails": {
        "allowed_tools": ["sftp_transfer", "api_upload", "s3_presigned_url"],
        "credential_scope": "refresh_only",
        "time_budget_minutes": 30,
        "approval_required_for": ["unlisted_endpoints"]
    },
    "context": {
        "file_path": "/data/export_20261013.csv",
        "destination": "partner-system",
        "deadline": "2026-10-13T17:00:00Z"
    }
}

# Orchestrator loop
while not mission_complete(mission):
    reasoning_step = agent.reason(mission, context, trace)
    if violates_guardrails(reasoning_step, mission.guardrails):
        trace.append({"step": "rejected", "reason": "guardrail violation"})
        continue
    result = execute_tool(reasoning_step.action, reasoning_step.params)
    trace.append({"step": reasoning_step.step, "action": reasoning_step.action, "result": result})
    context.update(result)
    checkpoint(mission, trace, context)

The orchestrator does not know in advance whether the agent will use SFTP or an API. It enforces the guardrails and logs the trace. The agent decides the path.

Trade-Offs: When to Use MissionFlows

Use MissionFlows When Use Workflows When
The execution path depends on runtime context that cannot be predicted. The execution path is known and stable.
Failure recovery requires reasoning about the cause, not just retrying. Retry logic is simple and declarative.
The mission involves multiple systems with varying availability and capabilities. The systems and protocols are fixed.
You need adaptability more than reproducibility. You need reproducibility and deterministic debugging.

MissionFlows are not a replacement for workflows. They are a different abstraction for a different class of problem. If your pipeline is stable and the failure modes are well understood, a workflow is simpler and more debuggable. If your pipeline needs to adapt to changing conditions and the failure modes are unpredictable, a MissionFlow may be worth the complexity.

Technical Verdict

Use MissionFlows when the execution path cannot be predetermined and the agent needs to adapt based on runtime conditions. This applies to integration scenarios with multiple fallback options, incident response where the root cause is unknown, and data pipelines that span heterogeneous systems with varying availability.

Avoid MissionFlows when the execution path is stable and the failure modes are well understood. The observability and debugging complexity is higher. You lose the deterministic execution graph that makes workflows easy to reason about. If your pipeline runs the same way every time, a traditional workflow engine is simpler and more reliable.

Expect to invest in observability infrastructure. You need trace logs of reasoning steps, checkpoint management, guardrail enforcement, and escalation boundaries. The tooling for MissionFlows is less mature than for workflows. You will build custom instrumentation.

Start with guardrails. Without explicit constraints, agents explore unbounded search spaces. Define allowed tools, credential scope, time budgets, and approval gates before you deploy a MissionFlow to production.

  • From Workflows to MissionFlows (Dev.to)
raw.contentSnippet:
Traditional workflow engines assume the execution path is known before the first step runs. Airflow DAGs, Temporal workflows, and Prefect pipelines all encode a graph of tasks with edges that represent control flow. When step three fails, you retry step three. When a condition evaluates false, you follow the predefined else branch.
Agentic systems break that assumption. Instead of defining the path, you define a mission and let an LLM-backed agent decide the steps at runtime. If SFTP fails, the agent tries an API. If credentials expire, it refreshes them. If the primary endpoint is down, it selects a fallback. The mission stays constant. The execution path emerges.
This shift creates new infrastructure problems. How do you observe a workflow that writes itself? How do you version control execution logic that lives in prompts instead of YAML? How do you recover from failure when there is no predefined retry branch?
A workflow engine provides three guarantees:
Deterministic execution graph. You can visualize the DAG before it runs. Every node and edge is explicit.
Checkpoint boundaries. State is saved at task boundaries. Retry logic is declarative.
Audit trail. You know which tasks ran, in what order, and what they returned.
These guarantees make workflows debuggable. When a pipeline fails, you open the UI, see the red node, inspect the logs, and fix the task. The failure surface is bounded by the DAG structure.
A MissionFlow replaces the DAG with a goal and a set of guardrails. The agent receives a mission like "ensure this file reaches the destination securely before 17:00 and verify processing." It does not receive a list of steps.
The agent decides:
Which protocol to use (SFTP, API, S3 presigned URL).
How to handle credential expiration (refresh token, request new credentials, escalate to human).
What constitutes success (file transferred, checksum verified, downstream system acknowledged).
The execution path is not predetermined. It is discovered through reasoning steps that depend on runtime context: API availability, credential validity, network conditions, and the agent's interpretation of the mission.
This introduces three new failure modes:
Reasoning drift. The agent misinterprets the mission and pursues a path that satisfies the literal goal but violates implicit constraints.
Unbounded exploration. Without explicit guardrails, the agent may try dozens of approaches, consuming tokens and time without converging.
Non-reproducible failure. The same mission with the same inputs may produce different execution paths, making debugging harder.
Traditional workflow UIs render a graph with nodes colored green or red. You see the execution path at a glance. MissionFlows need a different observability model.
Instead of task boundaries, you log reasoning steps:
{
  "mission_id": "file-transfer-20261013-1847",
  "step": 3,
  "reasoning": "SFTP connection failed with timeout. Checking for alternative endpoints.",
  "action": "query_service_registry",
  "result": "found API endpoint with valid credentials",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-13T18:47:23Z"
}

Each step captures:
What the agent observed (SFTP timeout).
What it decided (query service registry).
What it did (called the registry API).
What it learned (found an alternative endpoint).
This log structure replaces the DAG visualization. You reconstruct the execution path by reading the trace.
Workflows checkpoint at task boundaries. MissionFlows need to checkpoint mid-reasoning because the agent may decide to pause, request human input, or wait for an external condition.
A checkpoint includes:
The mission definition.
The reasoning trace so far.
The current context (credentials, endpoints, partial results).
The agent's next planned action.
If the agent crashes or times out, you can resume from the last checkpoint. The agent re-reads the trace, re-evaluates the context, and continues.
Without explicit guardrails, an agent may pursue any path that satisfies the mission. Guardrails are constraints that limit the search space:
Allowed tools. The agent can call sftp_transfer, api_upload, and s3_presigned_url, but not ssh_exec.
Credential scope. The agent can refresh tokens but cannot request new API keys.
Time budget. The agent must complete the mission within 30 minutes or escalate.
Approval gates. If the agent wants to use a fallback endpoint not in the approved list, it must request human approval.
Guardrails are enforced by the orchestration layer, not the LLM. The agent proposes actions. The orchestrator checks them against the guardrails before execution.
In a workflow, retry logic is declarative:
task: transfer_file
  retry:
    max_attempts: 3
    backoff: exponential

In a MissionFlow, the agent decides whether to retry, try a different approach, or escalate. The orchestrator does not know in advance what "retry" means because the execution path is not fixed.
The agent observes a failure, reasons about the cause, and decides the next action:
If the failure is transient (network timeout), retry the same action.
If the failure is permanent (invalid credentials), try a different approach.
If the failure is ambiguous (500 error), inspect logs or query a monitoring system.
The orchestrator logs the agent's reasoning and enforces guardrails, but it does not dictate the recovery strategy.
When the agent cannot make progress, it escalates. Escalation is a guardrail:
If the agent has tried three different approaches and all failed, escalate to a human operator.
If the agent needs to use a tool outside the approved list, request approval.
If the mission deadline is approaching and the agent is not confident it can complete, escalate early.
Escalation boundaries prevent unbounded exploration. They turn a potentially infinite search into a bounded one with a human in the loop.
Workflows are versioned as code. You commit a YAML file to Git, and the workflow engine executes that version.
MissionFlows are versioned as prompts and guardrails. The mission definition includes:
The goal statement (natural language).
The guardrails (allowed tools, credential scope, time budget, approval gates).
The context schema (what information the agent receives at runtime).
Versioning a mission means versioning the prompt template and the guardrail configuration. Changes to the prompt can change the execution path without changing the code.
A workflow DAG is deterministic. The same inputs produce the same execution path. A MissionFlow is not. The same mission with the same inputs may produce different execution paths if the LLM's behavior changes (model update, temperature setting, token budget).
To mitigate prompt drift:
Pin the LLM version and parameters.
Log the full prompt and response for every reasoning step.
Run regression tests that validate the execution path for known scenarios.
Regression tests for MissionFlows are harder than for workflows because the execution path is not fixed. You test outcomes, not paths.
A MissionFlow system has three layers:



Layer
Responsibility




Orchestrator
Receives the mission, enforces guardrails, logs reasoning steps, manages checkpoints, handles escalation.


Agent
Receives the mission and context, reasons about the next action, proposes tool calls, interprets results.


Tool Layer
Executes actions (SFTP transfer, API call, database query), returns results to the agent.



The orchestrator is stateful. It maintains the mission state, the reasoning trace, and the checkpoint history. It does not reason. It enforces constraints and logs decisions.
The agent is stateless. It receives the mission, the current context, and the reasoning trace. It returns the next action. The orchestrator decides whether to execute that action based on guardrails.
The tool layer is also stateless. Each tool is a function that takes parameters and returns a result. Tools do not know about missions or agents. They are reusable primitives.
# Mission definition
mission = {
    "goal": "Transfer file to destination securely before 17:00 and verify processing",
    "guardrails": {
        "allowed_tools": ["sftp_transfer", "api_upload", "s3_presigned_url"],
        "credential_scope": "refresh_only",
        "time_budget_minutes": 30,
        "approval_required_for": ["unlisted_endpoints"]
    },
    "context": {
        "file_path": "/data/export_20261013.csv",
        "destination": "partner-system",
        "deadline": "2026-10-13T17:00:00Z"
    }
}

# Orchestrator loop
while not mission_complete(mission):
    reasoning_step = agent.reason(mission, context, trace)
    if violates_guardrails(reasoning_step, mission.guardrails):
        trace.append({"step": "rejected", "reason": "guardrail violation"})
        continue
    result = execute_tool(reasoning_step.action, reasoning_step.params)
    trace.append({"step": reasoning_step.step, "action": reasoning_step.action, "result": result})
    context.update(result)
    checkpoint(mission, trace, context)

The orchestrator does not know in advance whether the agent will use SFTP or an API. It enforces the guardrails and logs the trace. The agent decides the path.



Use MissionFlows When
Use Workflows When




The execution path depends on runtime context that cannot be predicted.
The execution path is known and stable.


Failure recovery requires reasoning about the cause, not just retrying.
Retry logic is simple and declarative.


The mission involves multiple systems with varying availability and capabilities.
The systems and protocols are fixed.


You need adaptability more than reproducibility.
You need reproducibility and deterministic debugging.



MissionFlows are not a replacement for workflows. They are a different abstraction for a different class of problem. If your pipeline is stable and the failure modes are well understood, a workflow is simpler and more debuggable. If your pipeline needs to adapt to changing conditions and the failure modes are unpredictable, a MissionFlow may be worth the complexity.
Use MissionFlows when the execution path cannot be predetermined and the agent needs to adapt based on runtime conditions. This applies to integration scenarios with multiple fallback options, incident response where the root cause is unknown, and data pipelines that span heterogeneous systems with varying availability.
Avoid MissionFlows when the execution path is stable and the failure modes are well understood. The observability and debugging complexity is higher. You lose the deterministic execution graph that makes workflows easy to reason about. If your pipeline runs the same way every time, a traditional workflow engine is simpler and more reliable.
Expect to invest in observability infrastructure. You need trace logs of reasoning steps, checkpoint management, guardrail enforcement, and escalation boundaries. The tooling for MissionFlows is less mature than for workflows. You will build custom instrumentation.
Start with guardrails. Without explicit constraints, agents explore unbounded search spaces. Define allowed tools, credential scope, time budgets, and approval gates before you deploy a MissionFlow to production.

That decision runs through Qwen,
author: Edmund DSouza

raw.creator: Edmund DSouza
raw.title: How Qwen Powers REGLO Agent’s On-Chain Decisions
raw.dc:creator: Edmund DSouza
raw.content:
REGLO Agent is an AI agent built for the Monad Metropolis hackathon that gets paid automatically in MON when it proves — on-chain — that it saved money by scheduling compute around real solar-curtailment windows. The reasoning step — deciding which window to act on, out of dozens of real candidates, and explaining why — is where Qwen comes in.

Where Qwen fits in

REGLO Agent evaluates real curtailment and tariff data from REGLO (a live solar-curtailment monitoring platform covering four UK solar sites) and has to pick the best window to defer a compute job into. That decision runs through Qwen, Alibaba Cloud’s LLM, called via DashScope’s OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint in agent/reason.js. Setting REASONING_PROVIDER=qwen routes every decision through Qwen for that run.

Qwen receives the full list of candidate windows — site, hour, curtailment risk, tariff — and returns both a choice and a plain-language rationale. On a real run, Qwen explained its pick as “the 13:00 slot has the lowest electricity price, and all sites carry the same low curtailment risk, so it’s the cheapest available choice” — reasoning that’s checkable against the raw numbers in seconds, not a black box.

What value that actually brings

Two things, concretely. First, interpretability: the contract and the oracle never read the LLM’s wording — they independently verify the real cost saving before any payout happens — but Qwen’s explanation is the only human-readable part of the whole pipeline, which matters for anyone (a user, a judge) trying to understand why the agent acted. Second, a built-in honesty check: every run also computes the deterministic cost-optimal window independently and compares it against Qwen’s pick. If Qwen’s answer isn’t actually the cheapest option, the agent logs that out loud rather than quietly trusting the model. On every real run so far, Qwen’s pick has matched the true optimum.

Architecturally, Qwen never touches the numbers that decide the payout — it only picks which window to act on. An oracle independently re-derives the baseline and actual cost from REGLO’s real data and signs that; the smart contract checks the saving itself before paying out. A wrong or hallucinated answer from Qwen could at worst mean a smaller saving — never a wrong or fraudulent payout. That separation is what makes it safe to let an LLM make a real-money decision at all.

Proof, not a claim

A real run against real REGLO data, reasoning through Qwen, produced a real payout on Monad testnet: 0x666c6090caba0282d6b96c148c6206cd0778635eb2f2131e0a063ee77c99b09a. The same code path also supports Kimi and a local Ollama fallback, so the agent keeps working even if one provider is unreachable — but for this run, every decision genuinely came from Qwen.

Full project: github.com/edmundjeevan/reglo-agent-pipeline

What I Built. Photograph the find, enter name brand category condition age and buy cost. Optionally upload sold-history CSV so estimates learn your niche. Get a listing draft from a local open-weight model, a fair-price range, and net payout, plus a profit dashboard. Who pays: resellers listing 20 to 50 items weekly, saving 10 minutes per listing.

Demo. Tested on Apple M2, Python 3.14. Clone repo, venv, pip install, ollama pull gemma3:1b, uvicorn app.main:app. Deploy to Render button in README. Verified live: Gemma wrote Canon AE-1 listing, p50 184.62, net 110.62, margin 59.9 pct on a 50 buy.

Code. https://github.com/firfircelik/flipprice. FastAPI plus single-page UI with photo upload, inventory, dashboard. Ollama inference, TabPFN pricing with Ridge fallback, local JSON or Atlas. Tests 7 of 7 green as user journeys: market flow, offline mode, hostile inputs, photo attach, live model test.

How I Built It. Describer: Gemma 3 via Ollama, constrained prompt, brand-first titles, local fallback chain. Pricing: TabPFN first, Ridge fallback after RandomForest failed monotonicity on 20-row CSVs. Sellers upload own CSV with validation. Note: TabPFN 9 needs one-time license plus token, then same code switches engines.

Why Open Matters. Closed APIs at 5 to 15 cents per listing erase margin at 50 listings a week. Local open weights cost near zero, work offline, keep data on device. TabPFN learns your own history. Open makes the unit economics work.

raw.title: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk
raw.summary:
Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk

Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs.

The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month".

The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275:

On Artificial Analysis it scores 38, just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA.

It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier.

Via Hacker News

Start dev server and open in browser

This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.

Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.

Talking to my computer

I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.

Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:

Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.

Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.

We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.

What we built

We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:

  • A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that
  • Four working imports:
    • The most recent Substack items via RSS
    • Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner
    • All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository
    • My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository
  • The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages
  • Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage
  • Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages
  • Integration with my site search engine

It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.

Finishing it with a review

Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.

I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.

You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

The end result

You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page, or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter.

The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.

GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.

Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver

OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.

I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.

This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.

I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.

I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!

The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

raw.dc:creator: vishnukool
raw.content:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.

You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo

We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.

One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.

Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.

Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:

* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.

* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.

* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.

* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.

We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.

Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.

I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.

If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.

Thanks!

https://agent37.com

author: akarale-nv

raw.title: viable/strict/1791882163: [Windows] Depend on PyPI CUDA runtime packages in wheels (#194056)
raw.author: akarale-nv
raw.content:
Summary

This PR teaches Windows PyTorch CUDA wheels to locate their CUDA runtime DLLs from installed NVIDIA PyPI packages (via cuda-pathfinder) rather than bundling them inside torch/lib/. It adds per-OS wheel dependency metadata, updates the build matrix generator, adjusts CMake to skip bundling when using PyPI-sourced runtimes, and adds a Windows smoke test that validates the declared cuda-toolkit version matches the build.

  • torch/__init__.py : On Windows CUDA builds, cuda-pathfinder is called to load each CUDA library

  • Build matrix / workflows: PYTORCH_EXTRA_INSTALL_REQUIREMENTS is restructured from flat strings to {linux, windows} dicts; Windows CUDA entries gain cuda-toolkit, cuda-pathfinder, nvidia-cudnn-cuXX, nvidia-cusparselt-cuXX, and nvidia-nvjitlink-cuXX requirements. CPU and macOS entries that incorrectly carried Linux-scoped requirements are cleaned up.
    Windows and Linux use different CUDA Toolkit patch versions and dependency sets, so the binary-workflow generator now represents those requirements independently.

  • cmake/PostBuildSteps.cmake: CUDA DLL bundling is conditionally skipped for PyPI wheel builds; NvToolsExt install is moved outside that guard, so it is always included for CUDA builds regardless of packaging mode.

  • smoke_test.py: The Windows smoke test checks the full major.minor.patch CUDA Toolkit version because older CUPTI DLL naming does not provide compatible discovery across all patch versions. This is addressed upstream with future CTK versions.

Motivation

This reduces Windows torch wheel size to 277 MB and avoids cross-DLL-boundary problems when multiple Python packages in one process ship their own CUDA DLL copies. Relying on shared PyPI CUDA packages avoids duplicate runtime copies and improves mixed-package deployments.

Test Plan

  • Locally validated tests added to smoke_test.py.
  • Validate the packaging change in Windows x86 OOT CI and investigate additional failures.

Approved by: https://github.com/atalman

title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire

Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human
author: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink

raw.creator: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
raw.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
raw.dc:creator: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.12596v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

author: Wei Minn, Zhensu Sun, Lwin Khin Shar, David Lo

raw.creator: Wei Minn, Zhensu Sun, Lwin Khin Shar, David Lo
raw.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
raw.dc:creator: Wei Minn, Zhensu Sun, Lwin Khin Shar, David Lo
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.12569v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.

raw.creator: PENG YONG
raw.title: I built a face-rating tool that never sees your photo — here's what I learned about on-device ML
raw.dc:creator: PENG YONG
raw.content:
Why I Built This

A friend told me his face shape was better than mine.

I'm not going to argue with him — I have no data. So I went looking for one of those "what's your face shape" tools. Every single one wanted me to upload a photo of my face. To a server. Run by someone I don't know.

Look, I'm a developer. I know what happens to uploaded images. I've written the code that stores them. I did not want a photo of my own face sitting in someone's bucket with a Date.now() filename and an ACL I can't see.

So I built the version I wanted: one that measures your face and never uploads it. Not "we delete it after 24 hours" — the photo literally never leaves the browser tab. It goes into a canvas, MediaPipe reads it locally, and that's the end of it.

It's called FaceRuler. It's free. There's no sign-up — that part wasn't a growth decision, I was just too lazy to build auth for a tool that doesn't need an account.

The Stack

  • Next.js 16 (App Router)
  • MediaPipe FaceLandmarker — 478 landmarks, compiled to WASM; the model is ~3.6 MB and both it and the WASM runtime are served from my own origin
  • Cloudflare Workers via OpenNext, D1 for the few tables I actually need
  • A hosted checkout for the paid deep report (the free report is the whole measurement, not a teaser)

The part that matters: there is no server-side inference. Nothing to opt out of, nothing to trust me about. The network tab stays quiet.

The scoring is just math (that's the point)

Here's the decision that surprised people most: there is no LLM anywhere in the scoring.

I could have asked a model to "rate this face". I didn't, for two reasons. One, it would mean uploading the photo — dead on arrival. Two, a score you can't reproduce is a score you can't argue with, and people who use face-rating tools argue.

So it's geometry. Every sub-metric is scored with a Gaussian falloff around a reference target:

export const targetScore = (value: number, target: number, tol: number): number => {
  const z = (value - target) / tol;
  return 100 * Math.exp(-0.5 * z * z);
};

Eight sub-metrics (symmetry, facial thirds, FWHR, canthal tilt, jaw ratio, eye spacing, eye aspect, golden ratios) roll up into five weighted dimensions. The weighted overall maps onto the PSL 0–8 scale with a logistic curve anchored so an average face lands at exactly 4.0:

// overall 50 -> exactly 4.0 on the 0-8 scale
export const overallToPsl = (overall: number): number =>
  8 / (1 + Math.exp(-(overall - 50) / 13));

Median at 4.0, not 5 — the PSL scale is deliberately stricter than a casual 1–10 rating, and the percentile uses a normal distribution (mean 4.0, SD 0.9).

Because it's all pure functions, the entire engine is unit-tested (12/12 green) and "recalibrate" is a one-line change instead of a retrain. Same landmarks in, same report out, every single time.

Two things that were harder than they look

MediaPipe coordinates will quietly shrink your face. The landmarks come back normalized: x divided by image width, y divided by image height. Compute a height/width ratio naively and a 3:4 portrait reads about 25% "shorter" than the same face on a square canvas — enough to flip the score. You have to scale the y component back into pixel-equivalent space. Nobody warns you about this one.

A tilted photo shouldn't change your score. So before computing anything, I measure the midline angle from forehead-top to chin and rotate every landmark into a roll-corrected frame. Vertical distances — like the FWHR numerator — fall apart without it.

One more that isn't a bug but deserves to be documented: the academic FWHR ratio (1.85–1.9) is measured on physical photographs. In normalized landmark space, the nasion-to-upper-lip distance runs ~36% of bizygomatic width, so the numbers aren't comparable at all. I calibrated my own center (2.75) from landmark batches instead of pretending the paper value applied.

The front-end bug that ate a whole evening

React 19's synthetic onChange does not fire for programmatically dispatched change events.

My upload component has to work for real users and for my own automated tests, which inject a File via DataTransfer. The synthetic handler was silent in the injected path. Real users would have been fine — which is exactly why it's dangerous. The test would have lied to me.

Fix: drop the synthetic handler, wire a native addEventListener through a ref. Turns out it's more robust for real users too.

And a rule I now enforce everywhere: never put a ref-dependent DOM node inside a conditional render. My result <canvas> lived inside report && (...). Before the first report, canvasRef.current is null, the draw function's guard returns early, and you get… nothing. No error, no output. I hit this exact bug twice, in two different components, before writing it down as a rule.

What's Next

  • Server-side license verification. Right now entitlements live in localStorage, which means clearing your cache loses your purchase. I say that out loud in the docs instead of hiding it.
  • A second tool that shares the same credit system.
  • Quarterly recalibration from anonymous aggregate data.

Try It

It's live and free, no sign-up: https://faceruler.com

Drop in a photo and you get your face shape, a PSL score, a percentile, and all eight metric readings — with the formulas behind each number instead of just a verdict. Your photo stays on your machine; you can watch the network tab if you don't believe me.

Genuinely curious: if you've shipped something where "we don't upload it" is the entire pitch, how did you get people to believe you? I ended up showing the calculation, but I'm not convinced that's the best answer.

raw.title: The Persistence Layer — Or, the Daemon You Never Agreed to Run
raw.dc:creator: goodpa
raw.content:
Last time I named the exit as its own layer (#58) — the cost of leaving is the layer that decides whether "own" was ever a choice. Today I want to go one floor down and name the thing that makes exit hard in the first place: persistence. Not whether you can leave, but whether the thing you installed will actually stop.

The headline that made me write this

A post climbed the board today plainly describing the behaviour: the Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default (446 pts). Read that literally. You ran a command once to use a tool; in exchange, something now lives on your machine, starts itself, updates itself, and keeps its own schedule. You didn't sign up for a process. You got a tenant.

That single behaviour is the quiet architecture underneath a dozen choices you think you're making freely. And it's not one product's quirk — it's the direction of the whole field.

Why persistence is its own layer

Every other layer assumes you're running the thing. Persistence is about what's running when you're not looking — and who holds the switch for it.

  • It survives your decisions. A daemon set to auto-start and self-update has a lifetime you didn't budget. Uninstalling the app is not the same as removing the daemon; the state you'd need to know about isn't in the directory you can see.
  • It changes after you vetted it. You evaluated version 1. It ships version 1.0.7 next Tuesday by itself. Your approval was for a snapshot; you're now running a moving target with your name on the config.
  • It holds privileges you granted once. The token, the key, the filesystem scope, the network egress — all authorised at install time, all still live. Access you don't renew is access you don't audit.
  • It becomes the default, and defaults are sticky. When "install a persistent agent" is the out-of-the-box path, the careful version is the one you have to opt out of. That is a choice made for you.

The tell: consent at install, drift forever

Consent in software is a point event — a click at install — while behaviour is continuous. Everything that matters happens in the gap between the two. The friendly word for it is "convenience." The accurate word is that your machine now runs code whose current behaviour nobody has re-approved, under a permission you can't remember granting.

This is why the sandbox shows up next. A "Launch HN" today pitched low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents (96 pts) — isolation as a product, because letting autonomous code persist on your box uncontained is now obviously a liability. And a quieter post showed the self-hosted counter-move: turning an ordinary WiFi 7 router into a software-defined radio (254 pts), or streaming expert weights off an SSD to run models larger than RAM (18 pts). The pattern: the machine you own, doing exactly what you told it, and nothing else.

What to actually do

  • Inventory what persists. List the daemons, launch agents, cron jobs, and auto-updaters on the machine — not the apps you opened, the processes that survive reboots. If you can't list them, they're unmanaged by definition.
  • Separate run-once from run-forever. A tool you invoke and a service that greets you at boot are different trust levels. Pay for the difference; don't accept it as a default.
  • Turn off silent updates for anything privileged. You may accept auto-update for a browser tab. For something with a token and network access, "surprise changes" is a vulnerability, not a feature.
  • Revoke access when the job ends. Access granted for a task should die with the task — the identity lesson (#47) and the access lesson (#48), compressed into a habit.
  • Sandbox what acts on its own. Anything that runs unattended, untrusted, and repeatedly belongs in a container with a kill switch and a resource ceiling (#50). Isolation is cheaper than an incident.
  • Know the uninstall path before you install. If you can't describe how to fully remove it — process, state, credentials, scheduled tasks — you haven't evaluated it, you've auditioned it.

The one-line version

Persistence is a layer because it outlives the moment you chose it. You can measure your exit cost (#58), hold your own data (#52), run your own runtime (#51) — and still be quietly governed by a process you forgot you agreed to. The layer you don't own is the layer that owns you, and the daemon is the layer that keeps running after you stop paying attention.

title: Building a Distributed GPU Cluster for LLM Inference on Idle Apple Silicon Macs
summary: A single M2 Max Mac Studio can serve 8‑token‑per‑second Llama‑2‑7B inference, yet most developers leave that compute idle overnight. ## Inventory and Network Topology arp-scan --localnet | grep -i apple returns MAC addresses and hostnames. In a typical lab you might see two M2 Max units (38‑core GPU, 400 GB/s bandwidth), one M3 Ultra (80‑core GPU, 800 GB/s), and one M1 Pro (16‑core GPU). Record each host, its GPU core count, and unified memory size in a YAML inventory. Then run exo cluster init --config inventory.yaml on every node so Exo can build a peer‑to‑peer mesh over mDNS. Action: Create
author: lucanu

raw.creator: lucanu
raw.title: Building a Distributed GPU Cluster for LLM Inference on Idle Apple Silicon Macs
raw.dc:creator: lucanu
raw.content:
A single M2 Max Mac Studio can serve 8‑token‑per‑second Llama‑2‑7B inference, yet most developers leave that compute idle overnight. ## Inventory and Network Topology
Start by enumerating every Apple Silicon machine on the LAN. arp-scan --localnet | grep -i apple returns MAC addresses and hostnames. In a typical lab you might see two M2 Max units (38‑core GPU, 400 GB/s bandwidth), one M3 Ultra (80‑core GPU, 800 GB/s), and one M1 Pro (16‑core GPU). Record each host, its GPU core count, and unified memory size in a YAML inventory. Then run exo cluster init --config inventory.yaml on every node so Exo can build a peer‑to‑peer mesh over mDNS. Action: Create an inventory YAML and run exo cluster init --config inventory.yaml on each Mac to join the cluster. ## Unified Memory as a Shared Tensor Buffer
Apple’s unified memory lets the CPU and GPU address the same physical pages, eliminating PCIe copies. llama.cpp 0.3.0 exploits this with --n-gpu-layers. On an M2 Max you can offload 35 of 32 layers for a 7 B model: ./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 4096 --n-gpu-layers 35 --port 8080. The same binary on an M3 Ultra can push all 32 layers (--n-gpu-layers 32) because the 80‑core GPU holds the full weight set. Verify layer residency with llama-server -m model.gguf --verbose 2>&1 | grep "gpu_layers". Action: Set --n-gpu-layers to the maximum layers that fit in GPU memory on each model. ## Orchestration with Ray and Exo
Ray handles request routing while Exo shards the model across the mesh. Launch the head on the most powerful node: ray start --head --port=6379 --dashboard-host=0.0.0.0. On every worker run ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379 --resources='{"GPU": 1}'. Deploy a Ray Serve entry point that forwards each prompt to the actor with the lowest queue length:

@serve.deployment(ray_actor_options={"num_gpus": 0.25})
class Llama:
 def __init__(self):
 self.llm = LlamaCPP(model_path="model.gguf", n_gpu_layers=35)
 async def __call__(self, request):
 return self.llm(request.json()["prompt"])

Action: Deploy a Ray Serve deployment that routes requests to the least‑loaded GPU using ray_actor_options={'num_gpus': 0.25}. ## Monitoring, Autoscaling, and Cost Accounting
Collect GPU utilization with Apple’s powermetrics: sudo powermetrics --samplers gpu_power -i 1000 -n 1. Feed the output to a custom Prometheus exporter (mac_gpu_exporter) that scrapes every 10 seconds. Four Macs drawing ~120 W total cost roughly $0.015 /kWh at US average rates, so a 24‑hour run costs under $0.04. Add an alert rule: avg_over_time(mac_gpu_utilization[5m]) > 0.8 to trigger autoscaling via a simple launchd job that wakes sleeping Macs. Action: Add a Prometheus scrape config for mac_gpu_exporter and alert when average utilization exceeds 80% for 5 min. Start tonight by running exo cluster init on every idle Mac and point a single Ray Serve endpoint at the cluster; you will have a working distributed inference pool before the next morning.

If this was useful: I packaged a deeper version as Prompt Engineering for AI Roles: Hiring Manager & Engineer Guide.

This article was drafted with AI assistance.

title: 일본어 학습 없이 일본어판도 1위: S1MB 영어·일본어 2관왕 Darwin ZTC
summary: 요약(TL;DR): 디시전 AI 공개 리더보드 S1MB에 일본어판(japanese-v1, 27개 벤치)이 추가됐고, Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5가 Borda 84.57로 1위에 올랐다. 2위 퍼플렉시티(80.86)를 3.71점, 4위 Jev 1.13(75.43)을 크게 앞섰다. 같은 모델이 영어판도 1위(90.80, 160개 모델)라 영어·일본어 2관왕이다. 핵심은 일본어 전용 학습을 하지 않았는데도 1위라는 점이다. Darwin ZTC는 영어 판정 엔진으로 학습됐다. 일본어 판정 학습셋을 따로 주지 않았다. 그런데도 일본어판 1위다. 좋은 판정가에게 필요한 능력, 즉 함정 문장 추론, 도덕 판단, 확률 보정이 일본어로 그대로 옮겨 갔다. 판정 능력이 한 언어의 패턴 암기가 아니라 옮겨지는 실력이라는 뜻이다. 여러 언어로 서비스하는 팀에게 바로 쓸모 있는 신호다. Borda 84.57 (2위 대비 +3.71), 과제 평균 60.05 (3위 대비 +1.62) 27개 벤치 중 10개 1위, 16개 top3 상위 3개 경쟁 모델과 일대일 모두 우세: 퍼플렉시티 15승 9패 3무, torchcast 15승 11패 1무, Jev 1.13 15승 10패 2무 JMM

  • 상위 3개 경쟁 모델과 일대일 모두 우세: 퍼플렉시티 15승 9패 3무, torchcast 15승 11패 1무, Jev 1.13 15승 10패 2무

대표 승리 벤치마크

  • JMMLU(일본 지식 시험) 88.4 공동 최고
  • 상식 도덕 판단 88.0 1위
  • SOBACO(일본 문화 상식) 72.5 1위
  • JaNLI(함정 문장 추론) 83.7
  • JSICK 문장 유사도 56.6
  • 운영자 생성 수학·형식 논리 3유형 모두 1위

왜 2관왕이 중요한가

응답 채점, 난이도별 라우팅, 위험 출력 차단은 서비스하는 모든 언어에서 매일 일어난다. 언어를 넘어 전이되는 판정 엔진은 다국어 확장 비용을 낮춘다. Darwin ZTC는 출력 토큰 0개, 순전파 한 번으로 판정해 지연과 비용도 낮다.

자주 묻는 질문(FAQ)

일본어 판정 데이터로 추가 학습했나?
아니다. 영어 판정 엔진으로 학습했고, 일본어 1위는 전이 결과다.

어디서 확인하나?
일본어판 https://hotchpotch-s1mb-leaderboard.hf.space/?category=japanese-v1 · 영어판 ?category=english-v1

바로 써볼 수 있나?
Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5는 허깅페이스 트랜스포머스 판정 서비스 기능에서 별도 코드 없이 실행되도록 공개돼 있다.

더 읽기

  • 비드래프트 기술 노트: 생성 없이 판정하는 ZTC 구조
  • 비드래프트 기술 노트: S1MB 영어판 1위의 의미

raw.title: Trained Only in English, #1 in Japanese Too: Darwin ZTC on S1MB
raw.dc:creator: AI OpenFree
raw.content:
TL;DR: The S1MB decision-model leaderboard now has a Japanese track. Darwin-27B-ZTC-v5 took first place there with a Borda score of 84.57, ahead of Perplexity (80.86), torchcast (80.49), and Jev 1.13 (75.43). The same model is also first on the English track (90.80 across 160 models). The striking part: it received no Japanese-specific training. Decision skills learned in English transferred to Japanese.

What is S1MB and the Japanese track?

S1MB (System One Mosaic Benchmark) scores decision models, models that return a judgment instead of generated text, across many specialized benchmarks and averages the per-benchmark ranks into one Borda score. The operator added a Japanese track (japanese-v1, 27 benchmarks) and measured the models directly. Live board: https://hotchpotch-s1mb-leaderboard.hf.space/?category=japanese-v1

The result

  • Borda 84.57, which is 3.71 points ahead of second place.
  • Task average 60.05, ahead of the next model at 58.43.
  • First place on 10 of 27 benchmarks, top three on 16 of 27.

Why cross-lingual transfer matters here

Darwin ZTC was trained as a decision engine in English. It was not given a Japanese decision-training set. Yet the capabilities that make a good judge, reasoning over traps, moral judgment, and probability calibration, carried over to Japanese almost intact.

That is the useful signal for anyone deploying decision models in more than one language: a strong judge is not just memorizing one language's patterns. It is learning a transferable skill.

Head-to-head on the Japanese track

Against each of the top three competitors, Darwin ZTC wins the majority of benchmarks: 15 to 9 versus Perplexity, 15 to 11 versus torchcast, 15 to 10 versus Jev 1.13.

Selected wins:

  • JMMLU (Japanese knowledge exam): 88.4, tied best.
  • Commonsense moral judgment: 88.0, first.
  • SOBACO (Japanese cultural commonsense): 72.5, first.
  • JaNLI (Japanese natural-language inference with trap sentences): 83.7.
  • JSICK semantic relatedness: 56.6.
  • Operator-authored math and formal logic: first on all three types.

FAQ

Was the model fine-tuned on Japanese decision data?
No. It was trained as an English decision engine. The Japanese result comes from transfer.

What is a Borda score?
Each benchmark's ranking is converted to points and averaged, so no single task dominates the headline.

Where can I verify this?
On the public board: https://hotchpotch-s1mb-leaderboard.hf.space/?category=japanese-v1 and the English track at ?category=english-v1

Why does a two-language lead matter?
Routing, scoring, and safety gating run in every language a product serves. A judge that transfers lowers the cost of going multilingual.

Further reading

  • VIDRAFT Engineering Notes: Decision models that judge in one forward pass
  • VIDRAFT Engineering Notes: What first place on S1MB English means

summary: Most agent stacks pick one model and use it for everything. Tagging an email gets the same model as reviewing a contract. That works. author: Bobby Hall Jr

raw.creator: Bobby Hall Jr
raw.title: Google Launched the Gemini Agent. Let's Build a Tiny Model Router in TypeScript.
raw.dc:creator: Bobby Hall Jr
raw.content:
Most agent stacks pick one model and use it for everything.

Tagging an email gets the same model as reviewing a contract.

That works.

It is also like hiring a senior lawyer to sort your mail.

On October 8, 2026, at Gemini at Work 2026, Google Cloud announced the Gemini agent, which it calls "a universal agent for work." It plans the work, uses skills and tools, and connects to business systems.

One line in the launch stood out to me:

It chooses the best model for the job, has built-in cost controls, and most importantly, has the security, administration, and governance required by enterprise customers.

In his keynote remarks, Thomas Kurian added that the agent orchestrates across Google's Gemini models and Anthropic's Claude models today. He also said "the best model for the task is not always the largest one." Google also says the agent has built-in cost controls.

That distinction matters.

The agent and the model are now separate choices.

Something has to make that choice on every task.

Routing is a policy, not a vibe. If you can't print why a model was picked, you don't have a router.

So let's build a tiny version.

By the end, you'll run one command:

npx tsx router.ts

And watch seven example tasks get routed, paused, rejected, and resumed.

This is my small model of the idea. It is not how Google's Gemini agent works inside. Every model, price, and task below is made up.

Table of Contents

  1. The Problem
  2. Step 1: Describe the Models
  3. Step 2: Decide What Fits
  4. Step 3: Pick the Cheapest Fit
  5. Step 4: Enforce the Spend Cap
  6. Step 5: Run It
  7. Where It Breaks Down
  8. The Bigger Idea

1. The Problem

A router has to answer three questions per task.

Which models can do this at all?

Which one of those is cheapest?

Is there still budget to run it?

Most code answers only the first one, by hardcoding a model name.

Then the bill arrives, and it answers the third one for you.

Capability first. Price second. Budget last. The order is the design.

2. Step 1: Describe the Models

A model is just a few facts the router can compare.

type Tier = "small" | "medium" | "large";

type Model = { name: string; tier: Tier; usdPer1kTokens: number; maxContext: number; tools: boolean };

type Task = { id: string; project: string; need: Tier; tokens: number; tools?: boolean; override?: string };

type Route =
  | { kind: "run"; task: string; model: string; cost: number; why: string }
  | { kind: "paused"; task: string; model: string; cost: number; why: string }
  | { kind: "rejected"; task: string; why: string };

Each model has a tier, a price, a context limit, and a tools flag.

Each task says what tier it needs and how big it is.

override lets a human take the wheel.

Google said users can pick a model themselves. That felt worth keeping.

3. Step 2: Decide What Fits

Fit is a hard filter. No scoring yet.

const RANK: Record<Tier, number> = { small: 0, medium: 1, large: 2 };

const MODELS: Model[] = [
  { name: "mini", tier: "small", usdPer1kTokens: 0.0004, maxContext: 32_000, tools: false },
  { name: "mid", tier: "medium", usdPer1kTokens: 0.003, maxContext: 128_000, tools: true },
  { name: "big", tier: "large", usdPer1kTokens: 0.015, maxContext: 1_000_000, tools: true },
];

function fits(m: Model, t: Task): boolean {
  if (RANK[m.tier] < RANK[t.need]) return false;
  if (t.tokens > m.maxContext) return false;
  if (t.tools && !m.tools) return false;
  return true;
}

A model that is too small does not fit.

A model with too little context does not fit.

A task that needs tools needs a model with tools.

A cheap model that can't do the job isn't cheap. It's a retry with extra steps.

4. Step 3: Pick the Cheapest Fit

Now we sort what's left by price.

function cost(m: Model, t: Task): number {
  return Math.round((t.tokens / 1000) * m.usdPer1kTokens * 10_000) / 10_000;
}

function pick(t: Task): { model?: Model; why: string } {
  if (t.override) {
    const m = MODELS.find((x) => x.name === t.override);
    if (!m) return { why: `override "${t.override}" is not a known model` };
    if (!fits(m, t)) return { why: `override "${m.name}" does not fit this task` };
    return { model: m, why: "user override" };
  }
  const candidates = MODELS.filter((m) => fits(m, t)).sort((a, b) => cost(a, t) - cost(b, t));
  if (candidates.length === 0) return { why: "no model fits" };
  return { model: candidates[0], why: `cheapest model that fits (${candidates.length} fit)` };
}

An override still has to fit.

If someone forces a small model onto a huge task, the router says no.

An unknown model name is rejected, not guessed.

Otherwise the router takes the cheapest model that passed the filter.

Every result carries a why string.

That string is the whole point.

5. Step 4: Enforce the Spend Cap

Each project gets a cap. The ledger tracks spend.

class Ledger {
  spent = new Map<string, number>();
  constructor(private caps: Record<string, number>) {}

  route(t: Task): Route {
    const { model, why } = pick(t);
    if (!model) return { kind: "rejected", task: t.id, why };
    const c = cost(model, t);
    const spent = this.spent.get(t.project) ?? 0;
    const cap = this.caps[t.project] ?? 0;
    if (spent + c > cap) {
      return { kind: "paused", task: t.id, model: model.name, cost: c, why: `cap $${cap} would be hit (spent $${spent.toFixed(4)})` };
    }
    this.spent.set(t.project, Math.round((spent + c) * 10_000) / 10_000);
    return { kind: "run", task: t.id, model: model.name, cost: c, why };
  }

  raise(project: string, cap: number) {
    this.caps[project] = cap;
  }
}

The check happens before the task runs, not after.

If the next task would cross the cap, it pauses.

Paused is not failed.

The work waits for a human to raise the cap, and then it resumes.

Google says its agent ships built-in cost controls. This is my tiny version of one.

6. Step 5: Run It 

// ===== EXAMPLE INPUTS (made-up tasks, prices, and caps) =====
const tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "tag-email", project: "support", need: "small", tokens: 2_000 },
  { id: "draft-reply", project: "support", need: "medium", tokens: 6_000, tools: true },
  { id: "contract-review", project: "legal", need: "large", tokens: 180_000 },
  { id: "summarize-thread", project: "support", need: "small", tokens: 40_000 },
  { id: "quick-fix", project: "support", need: "small", tokens: 1_000, override: "big" },
  { id: "translate", project: "support", need: "small", tokens: 3_000, override: "gpt-x" },
  { id: "second-review", project: "legal", need: "large", tokens: 180_000 },
];

const TAG = { run: "[RUN]   ", paused: "[PAUSED]", rejected: "[REJECT]" } as const;

console.log("tiny-model-router demo");
const ledger = new Ledger({ support: 0.1, legal: 3 });
const paused: Task[] = [];
for (const t of tasks) {
  const r = ledger.route(t);
  const detail = r.kind === "rejected" ? r.why : `${r.model} $${r.cost.toFixed(4)}  ${r.why}`;
  console.log(`${TAG[r.kind]} ${t.id.padEnd(17)} ${detail}`);
  if (r.kind === "paused") paused.push(t);
}

console.log("\nraise legal cap to $6, resume paused work");
ledger.raise("legal", 6);
for (const t of paused) {
  const r = ledger.route(t);
  const detail = r.kind === "rejected" ? r.why : `${r.model} $${r.cost.toFixed(4)}  ${r.why}`;
  console.log(`${TAG[r.kind]} ${t.id.padEnd(17)} ${detail}`);
}
console.log("\nspent:", Object.fromEntries(ledger.spent));

Output:

tiny-model-router demo
[RUN]    tag-email         mini $0.0008  cheapest model that fits (3 fit)
[RUN]    draft-reply       mid $0.0180  cheapest model that fits (2 fit)
[RUN]    contract-review   big $2.7000  cheapest model that fits (1 fit)
[PAUSED] summarize-thread  mid $0.1200  cap $0.1 would be hit (spent $0.0188)
[RUN]    quick-fix         big $0.0150  user override
[REJECT] translate         override "gpt-x" is not a known model
[PAUSED] second-review     big $2.7000  cap $3 would be hit (spent $2.7000)

raise legal cap to $6, resume paused work
[PAUSED] summarize-thread  mid $0.1200  cap $0.1 would be hit (spent $0.0338)
[RUN]    second-review     big $2.7000  cheapest model that fits (1 fit)

spent: { support: 0.0338, legal: 5.4 }

Here is what happened.

tag-email fits all three models, so it gets mini.

draft-reply needs tools, so mini is out and mid wins.

contract-review needs the large tier. Only big fits.

summarize-thread is "small" work, but 40,000 tokens is past mini's context. So it routes to mid, and that would cross the support cap. Paused.

quick-fix is overridden to big. Allowed, and logged as an override.

translate asks for a model that does not exist. Rejected.

second-review would push legal past $3. Paused.

Then a human raises the legal cap, and second-review resumes.

summarize-thread stays paused, because nobody raised the support cap.

Correct. The router does not get to give itself a raise.

7. Where It Breaks Down

This is a teaching model. Real routing is harder.

  • Tiers are a guess. Real tasks don't label themselves "small." You need a classifier, or a cheap first pass, to decide.
  • Prices are per token here. Real costs include tools, sandboxes, retries, and cached tokens.
  • No quality check. A real router should watch whether the cheap model's answers held up, and route up when they don't.
  • Estimates before the run. Token counts are known after the run. The cap check uses an estimate before it.
  • One ledger, one process. Real spend tracking is shared, and two tasks can race past a cap together.

None of those change the shape.

Filter by capability. Sort by price. Check the budget. Print why.

8. The Bigger Idea 

task
  └→ filter: tier, context, tools
       └→ sort: cheapest fit (or override)
            └→ ledger: under the cap?
                 ├→ run, with a reason
                 ├→ pause, until a human raises the cap
                 └→ reject, with a reason

The task provides the requirements.

The models provide the options.

The filter provides the floor.

The price provides the order.

The cap provides the ceiling.

The human provides the raise.

This part is prediction, not history.

I think "which model are you on?" is becoming the wrong question for agents. The model will change every few months. Google said almost exactly that in the launch.

The better question is: what is your routing policy, and can you read it?

Picking the model is now part of the job. So it should be part of the log.

Try Roster

I'm building Roster around this idea: AI employees with real responsibilities, tools, memory, schedules and computer access. Each one has a lane, and a budget that lane can't quietly outgrow.

If the same follow-ups, handoffs, and waiting loops keep eating your week, give them to an AI employee.

Try Roster →

summary: Every time I needed to rent a GPU, the workflow was the same: open six provider tabs, squint at pricing pages that all structure their numbers differently, and try to remember whether that H100 price was spot, on-demand, or a 3-year contract rate buried in a footnote. So I built the thing I wanted: a price index that normalizes GPU cloud pricing into one dataset, where every row says what kind of price it is and links back to the provider page it came from. Some of what the data shows right now (it refreshes hourly): GPU Cheapest $/hr Provider Price type H100 1.37 Vast.ai spot H200 2.62 CoreWe
author: Riley Calhoun

raw.creator: Riley Calhoun
raw.title: I got tired of checking GPU cloud pricing pages by hand, so I built a price index API
raw.dc:creator: Riley Calhoun
raw.content:
Every time I needed to rent a GPU, the workflow was the same: open six provider tabs, squint at pricing pages that all structure their numbers differently, and try to remember whether that H100 price was spot, on-demand, or a 3-year contract rate buried in a footnote.

So I built the thing I wanted: a price index that normalizes GPU cloud pricing into one dataset, where every row says what kind of price it is and links back to the provider page it came from.

Some of what the data shows right now (it refreshes hourly):

GPU Cheapest $/hr Provider Price type
H100 1.37 Vast.ai spot
H200 2.62 CoreWeave spot
A100 1.15 Paperspace 3-yr contract
L40S 0.79 RunPod community cloud
B200 4.26 CoreWeave spot

The price-type column is the part I care about most. A $1.15 A100 sounds cheaper than a $1.37 H100 until you notice one is a 3-year contract and the other is spot. Most comparison content flattens that away; the index doesn't.

The API is live on RapidAPI as GPU Index — there's a free tier (1,000 requests/month) if you want to poke at it: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/gpu-index1

Endpoints are simple: /prices for the full normalized dataset (filter by GPU family, provider, or price type), /summary for the cheapest price per family, /gpus and /providers for what's covered and how fresh each source is.

While I was in there, I built the same pattern for a few other datasets I kept checking by hand:

  • LLM Token Price Index — 458 models, per-token input/output prices normalized across providers. Same model, side by side: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/llm-token-price-index
  • Domain Price Index — registration/renewal/transfer prices per TLD, because renewal pricing is where registrars actually make their money: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/domain-price-index
  • CT Lookup — Certificate Transparency data as JSON, with a watchlist for catching certs issued for your domains that you didn't request: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/ct-lookup
  • Email Deliverability Check — one call returns SPF/DKIM/DMARC/MX/rDNS verdicts for a domain, with fix hints: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/email-deliverability-check

All of them have the same free tier, and every price row in the indexes carries its source URL so you can check my work. If you're building a router, a cost dashboard, or anything that picks compute or models programmatically, I'd rather you call an API than maintain your own scrapers — that was certainly true for me.

Feedback welcome: what provider or GPU family am I missing?
