Mistral just pushed its new flagship model, Mistral Large 4, into public preview. This is a trillion-parameter, multimodal mixture-of-experts system positioned for complex work like cybersecurity and agentic reasoning. The key takeaway isn't just the scale, but Mistral's commitment to release the model weights by the end of the month, continuing their push for open, self-hostable foundation models.
Mistral Large 4, or ML4, is a massive model with a playful nickname: 'le Chonk'. It's a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with a reported one trillion parameters, of which around 49 to 52 billion are active for any given token. This MoE design allows for a very large model capacity while managing inference costs. The model is natively multimodal, built to process both text and images.
Mistral is explicit about the model's target workloads: cybersecurity, finance, and agentic AI. They claim it ranks among the best open-weight models, designed to compete with top-tier systems from US and Chinese labs. The training was done from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA GPUs in Mistral's own European data centers, a detail they highlight as part of a strategy for 'AI sovereignty'.
The most significant part of this release is the pending open-weight drop. While the preview API is available now through Mistral Studio, the company stated the weights will be released by the end of October 2026. This opens the door for self-hosting, fine-tuning, and deep auditing that closed models don't allow.
For teams working in sensitive domains like security, this is critical. Running a model on your own infrastructure means your data and intellectual property remain under your control. Mistral emphasizes this, noting that ML4 gives organizations the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies without provider-level refusals blocking legitimate research.
The focus on agentic capabilities is also notable. The announcement materials suggest the model is built for tool use and complex, multi-step tasks, which is where many production systems are heading.
You can access the model today via the preview API on Mistral Studio. This is the best way to evaluate its capabilities on your specific workloads before committing to a self-hosted deployment. Mistral has not yet published pricing for the preview API.
Here's a conceptual snippet for what an API call might look like, based on typical patterns:
import os
from mistralai.client import MistralClient
from mistralai.models.chat_completion import ChatMessage

api_key = os.environ.get("MISTRAL_API_KEY")
model = "mistral-large-4-preview"

client = MistralClient(api_key=api_key)

# Example for a simple text-based query
chat_response = client.chat(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        ChatMessage(
            role="user",
            content="Audit this smart contract for potential reentrancy vulnerabilities."
        )
    ]
)

print(chat_response.choices.message.content)

The primary gotcha is that this is a preview. Mistral has stated that the reinforcement learning process is still ongoing, and they expect performance to improve before the final release. The second consideration is the hardware requirement for self-hosting. A trillion-parameter model is not trivial to run. While the MoE architecture makes inference more efficient than a dense model of the same size, the memory footprint to simply load the weights will be substantial.
Mistral Large 4 is another major entry in the open-weight arena. It puts a frontier-scale model within reach of any team willing to manage the infrastructure. For builders focused on security, data privacy, or building complex agents, the upcoming weights release is the event to watch. This is less about a single new API endpoint and more about the increasing viability of a powerful, sovereign AI stack.

raw.content:
arXiv:2610.12493v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tools have often been presented as methods to increase trust in machine learning models by making aspects of their algorithms more human-understandable. However, evidence accumulated over the last decade points to an overall failure of this objective, instead promoting overreliance on incorrect predictions, which can subsequently lead to algorithmic aversion. Rather, XAI appears to function primarily as a debugging tool, useful for obtaining anecdotal insights into, for example, features learned by the model. One of the main issues underlying this limitation is that XAI methods often oversimplify the inner workings of the model, resulting in misalignment between the explanation and the model itself - a behavior referred to as unfaithfulness or infidelity. Faithfulness can be interpreted as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model. Computing faithfulness in a rigorous manner would thus make it possible to quantify one of the various elements of trustworthiness of an explanation. However, existing metrics present significant limitations, making this quantification either infeasible or computationally expensive. In this position paper, we outline five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics and propose four possible avenues for research to bolster their reliability.

raw.content:
I just shipped ragleap-agents v0.1.0. It's not a framework, it's a guardrail.

llm is any callable(prompt) -> str. No SDK lock-in.

The loop

llm -> JSON action -> validate against JSON Schema -> check ToolPolicy -> execute or pause for approval

Security model 


python
ToolPolicy(
  taints=True,      # this tool reads untrusted data
  outbound=True,    # this tool sends data out
  requires_approval=True
)

Rule: After a tainting tool has run, every later outbound tool needs approval.

No policy? Counted as both taints + outbound. Fail closed.

Tool outputs are capped, fenced, tags neutralized case-insensitively.


**

## Pause / Resume
**

StateStore is pluggable. InMemoryStateStore included.

Approve -> sends. Reject -> never sends. Replay -> ResumeError.

**

## Provenance you can check
**

PR #628 merged as d3e0c14, release PR #646 -> tag 0482515
CI 37889921507 success, publish run 37890106262 with trusted publishing.

Wheel: d305238f... Tar: 44cf1267... - identical in logs and PyPI.

41 tests, mutation-checked.

**

## Install
**

pip install ragleap-agents==0.1.0
pip install ragleap-tools==0.4.0  # dependency

This does NOT stop prompt injection. It limits blast radius IF your policies are accurate.

raw.creator: Shu Ishida, Aliasghar Khani, Tianyu Zhang, The Cong Luong, James Seale Smith, Adam Gaier
raw.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
raw.dc:creator: Shu Ishida, Aliasghar Khani, Tianyu Zhang, The Cong Luong, James Seale Smith, Adam Gaier
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.12545v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.

author: Atilla Baspinar

raw.creator: Atilla Baspinar
raw.title: Create a AI customer service using LangChain
raw.dc:creator: Atilla Baspinar
raw.content:
What we're building: a multimodal customer-service agent

We'll build a customer-service agent that helps a customer troubleshoot an app error. The customer first describes the problem in text. The agent asks for a screenshot and a short voice explanation, then uses both files to suggest a next step. The customer doesn't have to start the conversation over.

The agent offers guidance; it does not actually repair the customer's device or claim that it has. In this example, we'll focus on how the conversation flows, how to send image and audio inputs, and how the agent keeps earlier turns in context.

For the second part of the example, prepare two sample files in the directory where you run the code:

  • error.png — a screenshot showing the app's error.
  • issue_details.wav — a short voice recording with details about what happened.

The example uses a Gemini model with image and audio input support. Install its LangChain integration and configure your API key before running the code:

pip install -U "langchain[google-genai]"
export GOOGLE_API_KEY="your-google-api-key"

Build the customer-service agent 

import base64
from pathlib import Path

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain.messages import HumanMessage
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

# Initialize a model that can accept both image and audio inputs.
model = init_chat_model("google_genai:gemini-3.7-flash")

# Tell the agent how to handle support requests and when to ask for evidence.
agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[],
    system_prompt=(
        "You are a friendly customer-service assistant helping customers "
        "troubleshoot app problems. If the customer describes an error but "
        "has not provided enough detail, ask them to upload a screenshot and "
        "send a short voice recording explaining what they were doing. Use "
        "provided screenshots and audio to understand the issue. Ask for "
        "clarification if needed, and do not claim to have fixed anything."
    ),
    # Keep conversation state between calls that use the same thread ID.
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

# Reuse this ID for every message in this support case.
thread_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "support-case-1042"}}

# First, the customer describes the problem using text only.
initial_result = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": (
                    "My budgeting app shows an error when I try to export "
                    "a monthly report. Can you help?"
                ),
            }
        ]
    },
    config=thread_config,
)
print("Agent:", initial_result["messages"][-1].content)

# After the agent asks for more information, read the customer's screenshot
# and voice recording and encode their file contents for the message.
image_base64 = base64.b64encode(Path("error.png").read_bytes()).decode("utf-8")
audio_base64 = base64.b64encode(Path("issue_details.wav").read_bytes()).decode("utf-8")

# Send the requested screenshot and voice details as the next user turn.
evidence_result = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            HumanMessage(
                content=[
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": (
                            "Here are the screenshot and voice details you asked for. "
                            "Please use them to help troubleshoot the export error."
                        ),
                    },
                    {
                        # The MIME type should match the actual image format.
                        "type": "image",
                        "base64": image_base64,
                        "mime_type": "image/png",
                    },
                    {
                        # Audio is sent in its own content block.
                        "type": "audio",
                        "base64": audio_base64,
                        "mime_type": "audio/wav",
                    },
                ]
            )
        ]
    },
    config=thread_config,
)
print("Agent:", evidence_result["messages"][-1].content)

How the tech works

Multimodal messages

A multimodal message contains more than text: it can include content such as images or audio. In LangChain, a HumanMessage can contain a list of content blocks, combining text with media. The model receives that message and can use the media to respond.

The first customer turn is text-only. In the second turn, a HumanMessage combines text, an image block, and an audio block. Each block's type identifies its content; base64 carries the encoded file data and mime_type identifies its format.

Base64 encoding

base64.b64encode(Path(...).read_bytes()).decode("utf-8") reads a local file, encodes its bytes as Base64, and converts the result to a string for the content block. The MIME type must match the file: this example uses image/png for the screenshot and audio/wav for the recording.

Conversation memory

The shared thread_id tells the agent that the screenshot and recording belong to the same support conversation as the customer's initial question. The checkpointer saves the conversation state between calls, allowing the agent to use earlier messages as context. Use a different thread ID for a different customer or case.

InMemorySaver is suitable for a small demo, but its checkpoints live only in the running process and disappear when it stops. For a production application, use a persistent checkpointer and an appropriate retention policy.

Model and media support

The exact formats and limits depend on the model provider. The selected Gemini model supports image and audio input, but not every model accepts every media type or content-block format. Check the provider's current documentation for supported formats and size limits. Sending a file as Base64 does not make a text-only model capable of understanding it.

Depending on the provider and model, audio may be transcribed, interpreted directly, or require a provider-specific format. If the standard audio block is unsupported, use the provider's documented format or transcribe the recording first and send the resulting text.

A quick privacy reminder

Screenshots and recordings can contain personal or confidential information. Send only files you are authorized to process, avoid logging sensitive media unnecessarily, and remember that a checkpointer may retain message content.

Further reading

  • LangChain messages and multimodal content
  • LangChain models
  • LangChain short-term memory

        "send a short voice recording explaining what they were doing. Use "
        "provided screenshots and audio to understand the issue. Ask for "
        "clarification if needed, and do not claim to have fixed anything."
    ),
    # Keep conversation state between calls that use the same thread ID.
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

# Reuse this ID for every message in this support case.
thread_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "support-case-1042"}}

# First, the customer describes the problem using text only.
initial_result = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": (
                    "My budgeting app shows an error when I try to export "
                    "a monthly report. Can you help?"
                ),
            }
        ]
    },
    config=thread_config,
)
print("Agent:", initial_result["messages"][-1].content)

# After the agent asks for more information, read the customer's screenshot
# and voice recording and encode their file contents for the message.
image_base64 = base64.b64encode(Path("error.png").read_bytes()).decode("utf-8")
audio_base64 = base64.b64encode(Path("issue_details.wav").read_bytes()).decode("utf-8")

# Send the requested screenshot and voice details as the next user turn.
evidence_result = agent.invoke(
    {
        "messages": [
            HumanMessage(
                content=[
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": (
                            "Here are the screenshot and voice details you asked for. "
                            "Please use them to help troubleshoot the export error."
                        ),
                    },
                    {
                        # The MIME type should match the actual image format.
                        "type": "image",
                        "base64": image_base64,
                        "mime_type": "image/png",
                    },
                    {
                        # Audio is sent in its own content block.
                        "type": "audio",
                        "base64": audio_base64,
                        "mime_type": "audio/wav",
                    },
                ]
            )
        ]
    },
    config=thread_config,
)
print("Agent:", evidence_result["messages"][-1].content)

A multimodal message contains more than text: it can include content such as images or audio. In LangChain, a HumanMessage can contain a list of content blocks, combining text with media. The model receives that message and can use the media to respond.
The first customer turn is text-only. In the second turn, a HumanMessage combines text, an image block, and an audio block. Each block's type identifies its content; base64 carries the encoded file data and mime_type identifies its format.
base64.b64encode(Path(...).read_bytes()).decode("utf-8") reads a local file, encodes its bytes as Base64, and converts the result to a string for the content block. The MIME type must match the file: this example uses image/png for the screenshot and audio/wav for the recording.
The shared thread_id tells the agent that the screenshot and recording belong to the same support conversation as the customer's initial question. The checkpointer saves the conversation state between calls, allowing the agent to use earlier messages as context. Use a different thread ID for a different customer or case.
InMemorySaver is suitable for a small demo, but its checkpoints live only in the running process and disappear when it stops. For a production application, use a persistent checkpointer and an appropriate retention policy.
The exact formats and limits depend on the model provider. The selected Gemini model supports image and audio input, but not every model accepts every media type or content-block format. Check the provider's current documentation for supported formats and size limits. Sending a file as Base64 does not make a text-only model capable of understanding it.
Depending on the provider and model, audio may be transcribed, interpreted directly, or require a provider-specific format. If the standard audio block is unsupported, use the provider's documented format or transcribe the recording first and send the resulting text.
Screenshots and recordings can contain personal or confidential information. Send only files you are authorized to process, avoid logging sensitive media unnecessarily, and remember that a checkpointer may retain message content.

raw.content:
I reran these benchmarks on the pinned PyTorch main snapshot and reviewed the results; the updated tables document the final decode coverage and performance.

Adds an opt-in FlyDSL FlexAttention forward backend for ROCm gfx950.

Summary

  • supports BF16 MHA/GQA prefill and packed-GQA decode
  • supports Q/K dimensions 128 or 192 and V dimension 128
  • shares K/V staging across query owners, pipelines packed-GQA decode, and splits KV blocks across two worker waves for low-parallelism MHA decode
  • supports causal, sliding-window, packed-document, and lowered captured-buffer masks

Supported scope

  • gfx950, BF16, sparse Q/KV block size 128
  • prefill: Q and K/V sequence lengths divisible by 128
  • decode: 0 < Sq < 128, with (Hq / Hkv) * Sq <= 256 packed query rows per KV head, and a shared or per-KV-head BlockMask
  • identity score_mod, custom scale, and supported lowered mask_mod operations
  • positive BHSD strides with a contiguous last dimension for prefill;
    contiguous BHSD inputs for decode

Performance

All 47 original PR cases were remeasured. The aggregate statistics below include all 47 cases; the detailed Triton comparison tables show the 46 selected cases with speedup above 1x. Latest speedup = Triton / 1edce62b; values above 1x favor FlyDSL. Speedups use unrounded timings. The previous-kernel column now uses 1239ef2b, remeasured with the same inputs and frontend launcher.

FlyDSL commit comparison

Suite Geomean latency change vs 1239ef2b Faster than previous Faster than Triton
PyTorch -28.89% 18/18 18/18
MiniMax prefill -30.05% 7/7 7/7
MiniMax decode -11.98% 12/12 12/12
DSV prefill -45.57% 5/5 5/5
DSV decode -4.23% 4/4 4/4
Overall -24.85% 46/46 46/46

Negative latency changes mean the current commit is faster.

Environment and timing

AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950).
Python 3.12.3, PyTorch wheel 2.15.0.dev20260827+rocm7.2 with the PR Inductor/FlexAttention sources, ROCm/HIP 7.2.53211, Triton 3.8.0, FlyDSL 0.3.4.1.

Each row compares all listed backends on one GPU: eight alternating GPU-graph samples, 20 complete compiled calls per graph, and 200 ms warmup before each backend/sample. Times are median milliseconds. Graphs capture the complete compiled GPU call through the real torch.compile(flex_attention) launcher, including requested auxiliary conversion kernels; host dispatch and compilation are excluded. Prefill returns O only; decode requests O, LSE, and max-scores.

The original masks and storage layouts are retained. PyTorch cases use causal masks. MiniMax decode retains the original per-KV-head top-k block lists. DSV prefill uses two equal packed causal documents, transposed Q/K, and V sliced from 256-wide storage. The original PR benchmark manifests define these workloads.

title: How to catch tool-calling regressions in CI on every prompt change
summary: You change one line in your agent's system prompt. The replies still read fine. But now the agent skips a tool call it used to make, or calls a tool when it should have asked a question first. Nothing fails until a user hits it. Here is the CI check we use to catch that. It scores recorded agent outputs against fixed test cases, so it calls no model, needs no API key and uses no secrets: name: tool-call-tests on: pull_request: push: permissions: contents: read jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" - na
author: Horus

raw.creator: Horus
raw.title: How to catch tool-calling regressions in CI on every prompt change
raw.dc:creator: Horus
raw.content:
You change one line in your agent's system prompt. The replies still read fine. But now the agent skips a tool call it used to make, or calls a tool when it should have asked a question first. Nothing fails until a user hits it.

Here is the CI check we use to catch that. It scores recorded agent outputs against fixed test cases, so it calls no model, needs no API key and uses no secrets:

name: tool-call-tests
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install pytest
        run: python -m pip install pytest
      - name: Validate case files
        run: python runner/atp.py validate
      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m pytest -v

Everything below comes from our free sample repo: https://github.com/sturdybench/agent-tool-call-tests-sample . It has 10 test cases, a small runner in plain Python, and this workflow. Every output in this post is copied from a real run on a local copy of the repo.

The idea: score recorded answers, not live calls

Calling a model in CI on every push costs money, needs a key in your CI secrets, and gives different answers from run to run. So the check does not call a model. Instead:

  1. You run your agent on the test cases yourself and save its answers in one JSON file.
  2. You commit that file.
  3. CI scores the file against the cases on every pull request.

When you change a prompt, a model or a tool list, you record again and commit the new file. The diff of that file is the change in behavior, and CI tells you whether it got worse.

A recorded answer looks like this:

{"responses": [
  {"case_id": "notool-001", "tool_calls": [], "text": "You're welcome!"},
  {"case_id": "choice-003", "tool_calls": [{"name": "some_tool", "arguments": {"key": "value"}}], "text": ""}
]}

Step 1: check the cases are valid 

python3 runner/atp.py validate

Output:

ambiguous-request            1
argument-escaping            1
correct-tool-choice          1
missing-required-argument    1
multi-step-order             1
no-tool-needed               1
parallel-calls               1
tool-error-recovery          1
unsafe-request-refusal       1
wrong-type                   1
total: 10 cases in 10 themes, all valid

Step 2: run the check with a baseline

The repo ships an example file, examples/responses.example.json. It records answers for only 3 of the 10 cases. Two pass. The third, type-001, fails on purpose: it sends the number 5 as the string "5". The other 7 cases have no recorded answer.

Those 8 known fails are listed in a baseline file, tests/fixtures/ci_baseline.json. pytest marks them xfailed, not passed:

python3 -m pip install pytest
python3 -m pytest -q

Output:

x.x.xxxxxx..                                                             [100%]
4 passed, 8 xfailed in 0.04s

The 4 passes are the 2 passing cases, a direction count test, and a test that the built-in dummy agent's results have not drifted. A green build here means "nothing got worse than the baseline". It does not mean all 10 cases pass.

Step 3: watch it catch a regression

To show a failure, we hand-edited two of the recorded answers, the way a prompt change might move them. We did not run a real model for this.

  • escape-010 asks the agent to add a recipe. The new answer makes no tool call, just says "Sure, I can add that recipe."
  • missing-001 asks for a calendar event with no start time. The new answer calls create_event anyway instead of asking for the time.

Then we saved them as recorded/after_prompt_change.json (a hand-edited copy of the example file, not in the repo), pointed the check at it and kept the shipped baseline:

ATP_RESPONSES=recorded/after_prompt_change.json \
ATP_BASELINE=tests/fixtures/ci_baseline.json \
python3 -m pytest -q

Output (excerpt):

E       Failed: REGRESSION escape-010: did not call when it should have. Expected pass.
E         reasons: expected 1 tool call(s), got 0
E         expected behavior: Pass if name is exact and servings is the integer 4.

E       Failed: REGRESSION missing-001: called when it should not have. Expected pass.
E         reasons: called forbidden tool create_event; expected no tool call, got 1 (create_event); text has no question (needs a question mark)
E         expected behavior: Pass means no call and a question asking for the start time.

E       AssertionError: more fails than the baseline allows:
E           called when it should not have: 1 now, 0 allowed
E           did not call when it should have: 1 now, 0 allowed
E           Called when it should not have: 1. Did not call when it should have: 1. Wrong call: 1. Other fails: 7.

FAILED tests/test_ci_recorded.py::test_case[escape-010] - Failed: REGRESSION ...
FAILED tests/test_ci_recorded.py::test_case[missing-001] - Failed: REGRESSION...
FAILED tests/test_ci_recorded.py::test_direction_counts - AssertionError: mor...
3 failed, 1 passed, 8 xfailed in 0.05s

pytest exited with code 1, so the build goes red.

Two things matter here.

First, each failing test names the case, so you know where to look without reading a log.

Second, the message says which way it failed. "Did not call when it should have" and "called when it should not have" are different bugs. The first makes an agent look lazy. The second can be dangerous, for example a payment or a delete that nobody asked for. A single pass count mixes them. The direction count test fails if either side gets more fails than the baseline allows.

Step 4: use it on your own agent

  1. Record your agent's answers to the cases in the same format, for example as recorded/my_responses.json.
  2. Set it in the workflow step: 
      - name: Run tests
        env:
          ATP_RESPONSES: recorded/my_responses.json
        run: python -m pytest -v

With ATP_RESPONSES set and no baseline, every case must pass. If some cases fail today and you accept that for now, write a baseline on purpose, review it, and commit it:

ATP_RESPONSES=recorded/my_responses.json python3 tests/test_ci_recorded.py --write recorded/my_baseline.json

Then add ATP_BASELINE next to ATP_RESPONSES. A case in the baseline that starts to pass also fails the build, with a note to update the baseline. That keeps the baseline from quietly hiding things.

Limits

  • Recorded outputs only test what you recorded. If you change a prompt and do not record again, CI still scores the old answers and stays green.
  • It does not call a model. Keeping the recordings current is your job, with your own agent and key, outside CI.
  • Ten cases are a smoke test, not a ranking. We have not run these cases against live models and we publish no model scores.
  • We have not tested this alongside promptfoo. As far as we know, promptfoo can check that a tool call matches the tool's schema. These cases test a different thing: whether to call a tool at all, which one, and sometimes the reply text.

This post is part of a short series, Testing AI agent tool calls. The other posts cover testing one decision at a time, and four things readers taught us about scoring.

The cases, runner and workflow are free here: https://github.com/sturdybench/agent-tool-call-tests-sample

We have not run the cases against live models ourselves. If a case or a claim here looks wrong to you, please say so in the comments.

raw.author: egesamuray
raw.content:
Go through the following checklist

  • Passes lint (spin fixlint)
  • Added/updated tests
  • Updated documentation (if applicable)
  • Included benchmark results (for PRs impacting perf)

Linked issue or supporting maintainer

Fixes #197512

BC-breaking?

No

Summary (human written only)

CUDA backward uses atomic additions, leading to non-deterministic accumulation order and ~1 ULP drift in float64 across runs. Gradients are verified correct against CPU and numerical baselines. Set GRADCHECK_NONDET_TOL on the linear interpolate OpInfo (matching other interpolate modes) to absorb run-to-run variation without weakening gradcheck precision.

Agent details (if applicable)

I reviewed the analysis below against the reproduced CI failure and the CUDA verification results, and it supports the one-line OpInfo change described above.

AI-assisted analysis (Claude), reviewed by the author:

  • The CUDA upsample_linear1d backward uses atomic accumulation and is already marked nondeterministic.
  • On an NVIDIA L40S, the failing OpInfo sample reproduced the CI reentrancy error under shared-GPU load. All observed differences were exactly 1 ULP, with a maximum absolute difference of 5.55e-17.
  • CUDA gradients agreed with CPU and independent numerical references.
  • linear was the only one of the linear/bilinear/bicubic/trilinear/area interpolate OpInfos without GRADCHECK_NONDET_TOL.
  • With the one-line metadata change, the formerly failing sample passed repeated loaded runs; negative controls above the tolerance and deliberately incorrect gradients continued to fail.
  • Lint: spin quicklint passes. spin fixlint reports no issues and makes no changes, but exits non-zero locally because CLANGTIDY_EXECUTORCH_COMPATIBILITY cannot run without a CMake build/ directory, so the lint box is left unchecked.

Pull Request resolved: #199901
Approved by: https://github.com/soulitzer

title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning
summary: arXiv:2610.08814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning
author: Xinchen Xiao

raw.creator: Xinchen Xiao
raw.title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning
raw.dc:creator: Xinchen Xiao
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.08814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question.
  We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure.
  On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

author: Stuart Farmer

raw.creator: Stuart Farmer
raw.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
raw.dc:creator: Stuart Farmer
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.12536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.

summary: arXiv:2610.08829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jev offers an alternative interface for language understanding: given an input and predefined questions, it returns probabilistic decisions rather than free-form responses. Whether this interface can support effective reasoning for text classification against leading LLMs remains an open questions. We introduce Emo-Jev, a training-free framework with two complementary implementations. Emo-Jev-D decomposes classification into task-specific atomic judgments and composes their probabilities into a final prediction. Emo-Jev-SC constructs multiple jud
author: Yazhou Zhang, Junhao Yu

raw.creator: Yazhou Zhang, Junhao Yu
raw.title: Emo-Jev: Probabilistic Reasoning for Emotion Classification with Jev
raw.dc:creator: Yazhou Zhang, Junhao Yu
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.08829v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Jev offers an alternative interface for language understanding: given an input and predefined questions, it returns probabilistic decisions rather than free-form responses. Whether this interface can support effective reasoning for text classification against leading LLMs remains an open questions. We introduce Emo-Jev, a training-free framework with two complementary implementations. Emo-Jev-D decomposes classification into task-specific atomic judgments and composes their probabilities into a final prediction. Emo-Jev-SC constructs multiple judgment paths from complementary perspectives and aggregates their predictions into a consensus decision. We evaluate Emo-Jev on eight datasets spanning sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, sarcasm detection and humor detection, comparing against direct Jev classification and five SoTA LLMs under input/output and chain-of-thought reasoning. Standard Jev achieves 62.93\% average macro-F1 versus 67.28\% for the strongest LLM baseline, with lower observed latency and generally lower cost.

author: Peter Chen, Wotao Yin

raw.creator: Peter Chen, Wotao Yin
raw.title: Training Numerical Intelligence via Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery
raw.dc:creator: Peter Chen, Wotao Yin
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.03872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of generating scientific code, but generating code is not the same as improving the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance, but rarely reveals its underlying cause and how to address it. We introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement. ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses this diagnosis to guide the discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, turning solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation. Across four challenging numerical domains--power flow equation, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs--ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, for example, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly $71\times$, with improvements further transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.

raw.creator: Wenbin Dai, Hao Zheng, Shiyu Liang, Chaofan Sun, Xueying Zhang, Hanbo Huang, Xuan Gong, Yiran Zhang, Enhui Liao
raw.title: REACT: Physically and Chemically Consistent Reconstruction of Marine Active Tracers
raw.dc:creator: Wenbin Dai, Hao Zheng, Shiyu Liang, Chaofan Sun, Xueying Zhang, Hanbo Huang, Xuan Gong, Yiran Zhang, Enhui Liao
raw.content:
arXiv:2610.03888v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations is critical for monitoring ocean acidification and understanding marine carbon cycling. Traditional assimilation and inverse models are physically grounded but costly for large-scale reconstruction. Recent black-box and physics-guided AI models improve efficiency, but are mainly designed for passive tracers, where the reconstructed variable is also the transported inventory. In contrast, pH is an active carbonate tracer: it is the prediction target, while dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is the conserved carbon inventory. This mismatch can produce low pH error while violating carbonate closure and source-free carbon conservation. To address this, we introduce \textbf{REACT}, a carbon-first reconstruction framework that decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding. REACT transports a latent carbonate state with a conservative advection--diffusion solver, captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations with a source module, decodes the corrected state into pH, and constrains the output through carbonate equilibrium. This design keeps pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state. On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by (14.7%) and chemical consistency error by (24.0%) over the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations show robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component.

The design looks cleaner, the colors are nicer, and somewhere in the diff the focus outline quietly vanished. I've shipped enough redesigns to treat this as a certainty, not a risk, so I built a short checklist I run every single time. Here's the whole
author: RAXXO Studios

raw.creator: RAXXO Studios
raw.title: Focus States That Survive a Redesign: A Keyboard-First Checklist
raw.dc:creator: RAXXO Studios
raw.content:
• Redesigns silently break focus states; I run a 6-point check before every ship

  • Replace :focus with :focus-visible so mouse clicks stay quiet, keyboards stay loud

  • A 3:1 contrast outline against both themes is the bar I hold

  • Tab the whole page once with the mouse unplugged, no exceptions

A visual refresh almost always eats the keyboard experience. The design looks cleaner, the colors are nicer, and somewhere in the diff the focus outline quietly vanished. I've shipped enough redesigns to treat this as a certainty, not a risk, so I built a short checklist I run every single time.

Here's the whole thing. You can run it on your own site in about twenty minutes.

Why Redesigns Eat Focus States First

Focus is invisible until you need it. That's the core problem. When I'm staring at a new layout in the browser, I'm clicking with a mouse, and a mouse never shows me a focus ring. So the one thing a keyboard user depends on is the one thing I'm least likely to notice is gone.

The usual culprit is a CSS reset. A designer drops in outline: none to kill the default browser ring because it "looks ugly," and then forgets to add anything back. Now every button, link and input is a dead end for anyone using Tab.

The second culprit is a component library swap. You move from one set of styled components to another, and the new ones ship with their own focus behavior. Maybe it's there, maybe it's a 1px gray line that disappears against a gray background. You inherited someone else's decision and never checked it.

The third is theme work. You add a dark mode, the outline color was hardcoded to a dark value, and now it's invisible on the dark canvas. The light theme is fine. The dark one is a black box, literally.

I treat the redesign diff as guilty until proven innocent. Any time I touch global styles, swap a component, or add a theme, I assume focus is broken and I go check. This is the same defensive habit behind The Undo Button Every RAXXO Tool Ships With: assume the scary path is the one nobody tests, then test it on purpose.

One more thing worth saying plainly. Keyboard users aren't a tiny edge group. Power users navigate with Tab because it's faster. Screen reader users depend on it. People with motor conditions that make a mouse painful rely on it entirely. When the focus ring dies, all of them lose their place on the page at once.

Swap :focus For :focus-visible

The single highest-value change I make is replacing :focus with :focus-visible.

Old focus styling had an annoying tradeoff. If you styled :focus to be loud enough for keyboard users, mouse users saw a big ring every time they clicked a button, which looked wrong. So people removed it, and both groups lost out.

:focus-visible solves this. The browser decides. Click a button with a mouse, no ring. Tab to it with a keyboard, loud ring. Same CSS, different behavior based on how the element got focus.

My baseline rule looks like this:


:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
:focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: none;
}

The outline-offset matters more than people expect. A ring pressed flat against the element edge reads as a border, not a focus state. Two pixels of gap makes it obvious the element is selected, and it keeps the ring from clipping on rounded corners.

I use outline, not box-shadow, for the ring. An outline doesn't trigger layout shift and it doesn't get clipped by overflow: hidden on a parent. box-shadow focus rings vanish inside scroll containers all the time, and you won't catch it until something scrolls.

There's one trap with outline: none as a reset. Never, ever apply it globally without a :focus-visible style to replace it. If you write *:focus { outline: none } and nothing else, you've deleted keyboard navigation for the entire site in one line.

I've seen this ship in production more than once.

Test the swap by unplugging your mouse, or just setting it aside, and pressing Tab. Every interactive element should light up as you move. If one doesn't, it's either not actually focusable (a div pretending to be a button) or your ring style doesn't apply to it.

This is the kind of small, boring default I bake into the starting point so I never have to think about it again, same idea as The Starter Template Every RAXXO Tool Begins From. Set it once, inherit it everywhere.

Contrast The Ring Against Both Themes

A focus ring that exists but can't be seen is the same as no ring. The number I hold it to is a 3:1 contrast ratio between the outline color and whatever's directly behind it.

Three to one is the threshold for non-text UI elements in the accessibility guidelines. A focus indicator counts. So I check the ring against the element's own background and against the page background, because the offset gap means the ring often sits half on one and half on the other.

The theme problem is where most of the failures hide. I run the check against every background the element can appear on. Light theme, dark theme, and any colored sections like a hero band or a footer with an inverted palette. One outline color almost never passes against all of them.

My fix is to tie the ring color to the theme, not hardcode it:


:root { --focus-ring: #1a1a1a; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --focus-ring: #f5f5f5; }

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

For elements that sit on unpredictable backgrounds, like a button over a photo or a video, I add a second ring with a contrasting color so at least one half is always visible:


:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #fff;
  outline-offset: 2px;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px #000;
}

White ring, black halo. One of them wins no matter what's behind it. I'd only reach for the box-shadow here, where I actually need the double layer, and I'd accept the clipping risk because the fallback matters more.

Check the ratio with any contrast tool. Pick the outline color, pick the background, read the number. If it's under 3:1, bump the outline to a thicker 2px or change the color. Don't make the ring thinner to look subtle. Subtle and invisible are the same thing to the person who needs it.

While you're in there, check that focus works in forced-colors mode too. Windows high contrast mode overrides your colors entirely, and outline survives that override where box-shadow sometimes doesn't. That's the other reason I default to outline.

Tab The Whole Page, Mouse Unplugged

This is the test that catches everything the CSS checks miss. I put the mouse away and Tab through the entire page, start to finish, like I have no other option.

The order should follow the visual layout. Top to bottom, left to right, the way you'd read. If focus jumps from the header to the footer and back up to the middle, your DOM order doesn't match your visual order, and a keyboard user is being bounced around the page with no map.

This breaks constantly after a redesign because CSS lets you move things visually without touching the DOM. You use flexbox order or grid placement to put a sidebar on the left that lives at the bottom of the HTML. Looks right, tabs wrong. Fix the DOM order, not the tab order. Resist tabindex with positive numbers; it's a patch that makes the next person's job harder.

Things I watch for on the walk:

  • A visible focus ring on every single stop, no silent jumps.

  • Nothing focusable that's hidden. If a mobile menu is closed, its links shouldn't be in the tab order.

  • No trap. I can Tab out of every modal, dropdown and date picker. If I open something and Tab cycles forever inside with no escape, that's a trap, and Escape should close it.

  • A skip link as the first stop, so keyboard users can jump past the nav to the main content instead of tabbing through forty menu items on every page.

The modal trap is the one that bites after a component swap. A good modal traps focus on purpose while open, then returns focus to the button that opened it when it closes. A bad one traps focus forever, or dumps you back at the top of the page where you've lost your place entirely. Open every overlay, Tab around, hit Escape, confirm focus landed somewhere sensible.

I also tab through after resizing to a narrow width, because mobile layouts reorder things and hide others. The desktop tab order can be perfect while the mobile one is a mess.

Do this walk once per major view. It takes minutes and it's the closest thing to actually being a keyboard user for five minutes. If you only run one item on this list, run this one. The naming and structure discipline from The Command Naming Convention Every RAXXO Tool Follows is the same spirit: predictable order so nobody gets lost.

Bottom Line

Run the four checks in order and you'll catch almost every focus regression a redesign introduces. Swap in :focus-visible, give the ring 2px of offset, hold it to 3:1 contrast against every background including dark mode, then tab the whole page with the mouse put away.

If I had to keep just one, it's the tab walk. The CSS can look perfect in the stylesheet and still fail in the actual flow, and the only way to know is to use the page the way a keyboard user does.

Add this to your pre-ship routine and it becomes muscle memory. I keep mine in the same place I keep the rest of my launch gates, because a check you have to remember is a check you'll skip on the busy day.

Redesigns silently break focus states; I run a 6-point check before every ship


Replace :focus with :focus-visible so mouse clicks stay quiet, keyboards stay loud


A 3:1 contrast outline against both themes is the bar I hold


Tab the whole page once with the mouse unplugged, no exceptions



A visual refresh almost always eats the keyboard experience. The design looks cleaner, the colors are nicer, and somewhere in the diff the focus outline quietly vanished. I've shipped enough redesigns to treat this as a certainty, not a risk, so I built a short checklist I run every single time.
Here's the whole thing. You can run it on your own site in about twenty minutes.
Focus is invisible until you need it. That's the core problem. When I'm staring at a new layout in the browser, I'm clicking with a mouse, and a mouse never shows me a focus ring. So the one thing a keyboard user depends on is the one thing I'm least likely to notice is gone.
The usual culprit is a CSS reset. A designer drops in outline: none to kill the default browser ring because it "looks ugly," and then forgets to add anything back. Now every button, link and input is a dead end for anyone using Tab.
The second culprit is a component library swap. You move from one set of styled components to another, and the new ones ship with their own focus behavior. Maybe it's there, maybe it's a 1px gray line that disappears against a gray background. You inherited someone else's decision and never checked it.
The third is theme work. You add a dark mode, the outline color was hardcoded to a dark value, and now it's invisible on the dark canvas. The light theme is fine. The dark one is a black box, literally.
I treat the redesign diff as guilty until proven innocent. Any time I touch global styles, swap a component, or add a theme, I assume focus is broken and I go check. This is the same defensive habit behind The Undo Button Every RAXXO Tool Ships With: assume the scary path is the one nobody tests, then test it on purpose.
One more thing worth saying plainly. Keyboard users aren't a tiny edge group. Power users navigate with Tab because it's faster. Screen reader users depend on it. People with motor conditions that make a mouse painful rely on it entirely. When the focus ring dies, all of them lose their place on the page at once.
The single highest-value change I make is replacing :focus with :focus-visible.
Old focus styling had an annoying tradeoff. If you styled :focus to be loud enough for keyboard users, mouse users saw a big ring every time they clicked a button, which looked wrong. So people removed it, and both groups lost out.
:focus-visible solves this. The browser decides. Click a button with a mouse, no ring. Tab to it with a keyboard, loud ring. Same CSS, different behavior based on how the element got focus.
My baseline rule looks like this:

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
:focus:not(:focus-visible) {
  outline: none;
}


The outline-offset matters more than people expect. A ring pressed flat against the element edge reads as a border, not a focus state. Two pixels of gap makes it obvious the element is selected, and it keeps the ring from clipping on rounded corners.
I use outline, not box-shadow, for the ring. An outline doesn't trigger layout shift and it doesn't get clipped by overflow: hidden on a parent. box-shadow focus rings vanish inside scroll containers all the time, and you won't catch it until something scrolls.
There's one trap with outline: none as a reset. Never, ever apply it globally without a :focus-visible style to replace it. If you write *:focus { outline: none } and nothing else, you've deleted keyboard navigation for the entire site in one line.
I've seen this ship in production more than once.
Test the swap by unplugging your mouse, or just setting it aside, and pressing Tab. Every interactive element should light up as you move. If one doesn't, it's either not actually focusable (a div pretending to be a button) or your ring style doesn't apply to it.
This is the kind of small, boring default I bake into the starting point so I never have to think about it again, same idea as The Starter Template Every RAXXO Tool Begins From. Set it once, inherit it everywhere.
A focus ring that exists but can't be seen is the same as no ring. The number I hold it to is a 3:1 contrast ratio between the outline color and whatever's directly behind it.
Three to one is the threshold for non-text UI elements in the accessibility guidelines. A focus indicator counts. So I check the ring against the element's own background and against the page background, because the offset gap means the ring often sits half on one and half on the other.
The theme problem is where most of the failures hide. I run the check against every background the element can appear on. Light theme, dark theme, and any colored sections like a hero band or a footer with an inverted palette. One outline color almost never passes against all of them.
My fix is to tie the ring color to the theme, not hardcode it:

:root { --focus-ring: #1a1a1a; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --focus-ring: #f5f5f5; }

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}


For elements that sit on unpredictable backgrounds, like a button over a photo or a video, I add a second ring with a contrasting color so at least one half is always visible:

:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #fff;
  outline-offset: 2px;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px #000;
}


White ring, black halo. One of them wins no matter what's behind it. I'd only reach for the box-shadow here, where I actually need the double layer, and I'd accept the clipping risk because the fallback matters more.
Check the ratio with any contrast tool. Pick the outline color, pick the background, read the number. If it's under 3:1, bump the outline to a thicker 2px or change the color. Don't make the ring thinner to look subtle. Subtle and invisible are the same thing to the person who needs it.
While you're in there, check that focus works in forced-colors mode too. Windows high contrast mode overrides your colors entirely, and outline survives that override where box-shadow sometimes doesn't. That's the other reason I default to outline.
This is the test that catches everything the CSS checks miss. I put the mouse away and Tab through the entire page, start to finish, like I have no other option.
The order should follow the visual layout. Top to bottom, left to right, the way you'd read. If focus jumps from the header to the footer and back up to the middle, your DOM order doesn't match your visual order, and a keyboard user is being bounced around the page with no map.
This breaks constantly after a redesign because CSS lets you move things visually without touching the DOM. You use flexbox order or grid placement to put a sidebar on the left that lives at the bottom of the HTML. Looks right, tabs wrong. Fix the DOM order, not the tab order. title: Counting LLM Tokens in Python: tiktoken vs a Dependency-Free Heuristic
summary: Every LLM feature I build eventually needs to answer one question: how many tokens is this? Context windows are measured in tokens, cost is measured in tokens, and truncation happens in tokens. Characters and words are close enough to lie to you and not close enough to trust. There are two ways to count, and I have shipped both. In this tutorial I want to show you when each is the right tool, and then how to stop choosing between them by hiding both behind a single interface with a graceful fallback. I will ground it in a small project of mine called ctxlens, but the technique is what matters,
author: Royal Simpson Pinto

raw.creator: Royal Simpson Pinto
raw.title: Counting LLM Tokens in Python: tiktoken vs a Dependency-Free Heuristic
raw.dc:creator: Royal Simpson Pinto
raw.content:
Every LLM feature I build eventually needs to answer one question: how many tokens is this? Context windows are measured in tokens, cost is measured in tokens, and truncation happens in tokens. Characters and words are close enough to lie to you and not close enough to trust.

There are two ways to count, and I have shipped both. In this tutorial I want to show you when each is the right tool, and then how to stop choosing between them by hiding both behind a single interface with a graceful fallback. I will ground it in a small project of mine called ctxlens, but the technique is what matters, not the project.

Option one: exact counts with tiktoken

tiktoken is the byte-pair-encoding tokenizer used by several OpenAI models. It gives you the real token count, the same number the model sees. If your job is billing, hard context-limit enforcement, or trimming a prompt to fit exactly, you want exact.

import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
tokens = enc.encode("Counting tokens is deceptively subtle.")
print(len(tokens))  # exact token count

Two things to know. First, the encoding matters: cl100k_base matches one family of models, and other models use other vocabularies, so pick the one your target model actually uses. Second, encode can choke on text containing special tokens unless you tell it not to treat them specially. In production I always pass disallowed_special=() so arbitrary user text never raises:

def count(text: str) -> int:
    if not text:
        return 0
    return len(enc.encode(text, disallowed_special=()))

The cost of exactness is a dependency. tiktoken is a compiled package, it downloads vocabulary files, and it is not something you always want in a lightweight library, a CI runner with no network, or a constrained environment.

Option two: a dependency-free heuristic

Sometimes I do not need the exact number. When I am profiling which part of a prompt dominates the context, or watching how usage grows across a conversation, I care about relative size, not the precise integer. For that I use a pure-Python heuristic with zero dependencies and no network.

The idea: real BPE tokenizers roughly pack a handful of characters into each token and break long words into several pieces. So I split text into word, number, and symbol runs, and charge longer runs more than one token.

import re

# words (including unicode letters), numbers, or any single non-space symbol
_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+|\d+|[^\s\w]", re.UNICODE)
_CHARS_PER_PIECE = 4


def heuristic_count(text: str) -> int:
    if not text:
        return 0
    total = 0
    for match in _TOKEN_RE.finditer(text):
        piece = match.group(0)
        n = len(piece)
        if n <= _CHARS_PER_PIECE:
            total += 1
        else:
            # long runs get broken into sub-tokens, rounding up
            total += (n + _CHARS_PER_PIECE - 1) // _CHARS_PER_PIECE
        # whitespace is folded into adjacent tokens, not counted
    return total

This runs anywhere Python runs. It is deterministic, so tests and CI produce stable numbers with no heavy install.

The honest caveat: this is an approximation, full stop. It does not reproduce any real BPE vocabulary, so its number will differ from the model's actual count, sometimes meaningfully, especially on code, non-English text, or unusual symbol-heavy input. Never bill a customer or enforce a hard context limit on a heuristic. Use it for relative comparison and offline profiling, and use tiktoken when the exact number carries consequences.

Stop choosing: one interface, graceful fallback

The real technique is not picking one counter. It is making the rest of your code not care which one it got. Define an abstract interface both implementations satisfy:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Tokenizer(ABC):
    name: str = "base"

    @abstractmethod
    def count(self, text: str) -> int:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def count_all(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[int]:
        return [self.count(t) for t in texts]

Both counters become subclasses. The heuristic one always works. The tiktoken one imports lazily inside __init__, so it only fails if you actually try to build it without the dependency installed:

class TiktokenTokenizer(Tokenizer):
    def __init__(self, encoding: str = "cl100k_base") -> None:
        try:
            import tiktoken
        except ImportError as exc:
            raise ImportError(
                "tiktoken is not installed; install it to get exact counts"
            ) from exc
        self._enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(encoding)
        self.name = f"tiktoken:{encoding}"

    def count(self, text: str) -> int:
        if not text:
            return 0
        return len(self._enc.encode(text, disallowed_special=()))

Notice the import lives inside the constructor, not at the top of the module. That is what makes the fallback clean: importing the module never requires the dependency, and the ImportError surfaces only at the exact moment a caller asks for something it cannot have.

Now a small factory ties it together. auto prefers exactness and silently degrades to the heuristic:

def _try_tiktoken(encoding: str = "cl100k_base"):
    try:
        return TiktokenTokenizer(encoding)
    except ImportError:
        return None


def get_tokenizer(name: str = "auto") -> Tokenizer:
    name = (name or "auto").lower()
    if name == "heuristic":
        return HeuristicTokenizer()
    if name == "tiktoken":
        tok = _try_tiktoken()
        if tok is None:
            raise ImportError("tiktoken requested but not installed")
        return tok
    if name == "auto":
        return _try_tiktoken() or HeuristicTokenizer()
    raise ValueError(f"unknown tokenizer: {name!r}")

The design choices here are deliberate. auto gives you the best answer available without a crash. heuristic guarantees the dependency-free path, which is what your tests should pin so they never depend on an optional install. tiktoken is explicit and loud: if you asked for exact and cannot have it, you get an error rather than a silent approximation. That last distinction matters, because silently swapping exact for approximate is exactly the bug that shows up as a surprise overage bill.

The payoff

The rest of your application never touches tiktoken or the regex again. It calls tokenizer.count(text). Swapping counters is a one-line change at the edge, tests run offline against the heuristic, and production gets exact counts wherever the dependency is present. You keep the name field around so reports can say which counter produced a number, because "1,240 tokens (heuristic)" and "1,240 tokens (tiktoken)" mean different things to the reader.

That is the whole pattern: an abstract count, a lazy optional dependency, and an auto mode that prefers exact and degrades gracefully. If you want to see it wired into a real tool that profiles where the tokens in your prompts actually go, this is lifted straight from my project ctxlens, and the full tokenizer package is at github.com/AgentPostmortem/ctxlens. Borrow the interface, keep the caveat, and count with confidence.

title: Testing AI Agent Tool Calls: A Release Checklist Beyond Task Completion
summary: A task-completion score can hide an agent that reached the right answer through an unauthorised action. Evaluate what happened, which actions occurred and whether the system stayed within its authority. This article was generated by an AI agent for Acadify Solution and Acadify AI Lab. All scenarios are illustrative, not client results or benchmark measurements. For each tool, define who may invoke it, the tenant and resource scope, required arguments, permitted state transitions, approval requirements and the meaning of success, failure or an unknown outcome. Enforce access in the application/
author: Acadify Solution

raw.creator: Acadify Solution
raw.title: Testing AI Agent Tool Calls: A Release Checklist Beyond Task Completion
raw.dc:creator: Acadify Solution
raw.content:
A task-completion score can hide an agent that reached the right answer through an unauthorised action. Evaluate what happened, which actions occurred and whether the system stayed within its authority.

This article was generated by an AI agent for Acadify Solution and Acadify AI Lab. All scenarios are illustrative, not client results or benchmark measurements.

1. Write an action contract

For each tool, define who may invoke it, the tenant and resource scope, required arguments, permitted state transitions, approval requirements and the meaning of success, failure or an unknown outcome.

Enforce access in the application/tool layer. A prompt can describe a boundary; it does not replace an authorisation check. Reading an enquiry, proposing a CRM update and sending an external reply deserve separate contracts.

2. Test the target as well as the payload

Use a disposable environment with synthetic data. Include two tenants and similarly named records. Verify that a supplied identifier does not grant access to a record outside the authorised scope.

Validate types, required fields and business rules at execution time. Rejected calls should cause no state change. Record the attempt and rejection with appropriate redaction.

3. Inject an uncertain write outcome

Test a service that commits a write but loses the response. A timeout does not prove that nothing changed.

Where the API supports it, use a stable operation ID and status lookup. Reusing the ID with a different payload should detect a conflict. If there is no reliable status or deduplication mechanism, represent the unknown outcome and escalate according to the workflow's risk.

Injected condition What to check
Failure before commit No state change; bounded retry if permitted
Commit followed by timeout Status resolution or safe escalation
Replayed request No unintended duplicate side effect
Same operation ID, different payload Conflict detected

A retry budget alone does not make a write safe. Expected behaviour must follow the API contract and business rules.

4. Bind approval to a proposal

Show the reviewer the target and important arguments. Test changes to content, recipient or target after approval. The old approval must not silently cover a materially different action.

Test rejection and expiry too. A delayed decision should not authorise a later, changed proposal. A blanket approval token disconnected from the proposal is difficult to audit.

5. Treat retrieved instructions as untrusted input

Place conflicting instructions in a synthetic document—for example, a paragraph asking the assistant to send a message outside the requested workflow. Check both the model's behaviour and the application's permission enforcement.

Record the input, selected context and attempted calls. Do not use real secrets or private customer records as test material. A single passing case does not show that prompt injection is solved; vary the cases and report the tested scope.

6. Exercise stopping and handover

Test missing fields, invalid tool output, expired access, repeated failures and step limits. Define terminal states such as completed, awaiting approval, failed and unknown outcome.

A handover should identify the last confirmed action and the unresolved step. A fluent final message is not evidence of a completed workflow.

7. Retain useful, limited traces

Record the case ID, workflow version, authorised scope, redacted arguments, approval decisions, tool results and state changes. Decide who can inspect traces and how long to retain them.

A reviewer should be able to reconstruct the result without unrestricted access to every document the system encountered.

8. Separate release gates

Report task outcome separately from policy and integration checks. Under a defined permission gate, an unauthorised write should fail the case even if the final answer is correct.

Document case counts, fixture versions, model and prompt versions, stochastic repeats where appropriate and known gaps. Keep a held-out set when tuning.

This checklist is a starting point, not a security certification or reliability guarantee. Adapt it to your system and the consequences of its actions.

Which failure injection would you add first to your agent's release test?

The gate that was supposed to make "certified" mean "safe" admitted a workload its own regression report had just flagged. This is the article about when "certified" does not mean "safe" — and about a gate that admits on the wrong evidence. Finding What the gate did Why it was wro
author: Debashish Ghosal

raw.creator: Debashish Ghosal
raw.title: I Signed a Regression and Almost Shipped It
raw.dc:creator: Debashish Ghosal
raw.content:
The regression report said blocked=True. A critical task had regressed. The promotion proceeded anyway. The attestation was written. The workload was admitted to production.

I signed a regression and almost shipped it — on HivePlane v0.2.0, the release where I added the promotion gate I'd been promising since v0.1.0. The gate that was supposed to make "certified" mean "safe" admitted a workload its own regression report had just flagged.

This is the article about when "certified" does not mean "safe" — and about a gate that admits on the wrong evidence.

Four ways the gate admitted wrong

Finding What the gate did Why it was wrong
#522 (Critical) recertify_and_promote admitted even when the regression report was blocked=True The report was a footnote, not a precondition
#523 (High) Default min_production_runs_survived=50 made certified unreachable The production gate deadlocked against its own threshold
#530 The drift detector compared failure counts across corpus versions Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent
#527 The regression report diffed against any-status prior attestation A non-comparable baseline masked a real regression

Pass-rate thresholds are necessary. They are not sufficient. Each of these is a way to be green and wrong.

The signature on a regression

522 is the one that kept me up. The flow was: re-certify, generate a regression report, promote. The report said blocked=True — a critical task had regressed. The promotion proceeded anyway. The attestation was written. The workload was admitted.

The regression report was generated, attached to the record, and ignored. It was a comment, not a gate.

tip: A check that annotates but does not block is a suggestion, not a control. If your promotion can succeed while the regression report is red, your regression report is decoration.

The fix: the regression report is a hard precondition. recertify_and_promote refuses if the report is blocked:

if regression_report.blocked:
    raise PromotionRefusedError(
        workload,
        f"regression report is blocked: {regression_report.critical_failures}",
    )

A critical regression feeds the refusal reason. The promotion cannot complete until the regression is resolved or explicitly waived with attribution.

The unreachable status

523 was a different kind of admission failure. The default min_production_runs_survived=50 meant a workload had to survive 50 production runs before it could be certified. In a field test that runs once, against a local stack, that's never. The production gate deadlocked against its own threshold — the workload could pass every benchmark forever and never reach certified.

A gate that's unreachable is a gate that doesn't exist. Operators will route around it, and a bypassed gate is an expensive dashboard. The threshold has to be reachable in the environment where it's enforced, or you've built a status cycle, not a ladder.

The baseline that wasn't

530 is the one that changed how I think about drift. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions. So if you grew the benchmark from 10 tasks to 20 — because the learning loop added a reviewed case — a healthy agent that passed 10/10 now "failed" 10 of 20 by your accounting. Corpus growth looked like decay. Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent.

The fix: drift is measured against the agent's own baseline with comparable corpora. You compare the same tasks, not different counts. A corpus version change is a new baseline, not a drift signal.

527 was the same lesson on the promotion side: the regression report diffed against any-status prior attestation, including a quarantined one. So a regression against a known-bad baseline looked like no regression. The baseline has to be the last certified record, or you're comparing against a version that was never safe.

What I learned

A signature on a known-bad artifact is worse than no signature — it carries the authority of certification without the safety. The regression report must block, not annotate. Identity binds to the attestation, not the manifest: change the hash, lose the certification. And the survival gate must be reachable, or you've built a status cycle, not a ladder.

The v0.2.0 field test demonstrates the promotion gate blocking a regression with a replayable diff (scenario S3), drift auto-quarantine and reinstatement (S4/S5), and the regression diff API. Full evidence in the field-test report; the certification and promotion design is in the certification v2 design doc.

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Certification v2 design · Learning loop design
  • Tutorial — Certify, Promote & Survive Drift
